News.title: Spain earthquake rocks Brit holiday hotspot Granada after massive tremors hit
News.content:
Spain earthquake rocks Brit holiday hotspot Granada after massive tremors hit

The popular Spanish holiday spot of Granada has been rocked by an earthquake which locals described as 'like an explosion'

Spain: CCTV captures sounds of earthquake in Granada

An earthquake has rocked the popular Spanish holiday spot of Granada with terrified locals reporting tremors that "felt like an explosion".

‌



The quake occurred 3.73 miles (6km) South of Granada at 3.46pm local time (2.46pm BST) sparking fear in the nearby city as “floors and walls moved”.

‌



The earthquake measured a magnitude of 3.7, according to the Mediterranean Seismological Centre, with its epicentre in the town of Ogíjares, at a depth of 6 kilometres.

‌



The quake was felt in several parts of Granada province as well as in several municipalities in Malaga province, Spanish news sources reported.

“It was rough here in Churriana de la Vega; I was asleep and went flying out of bed,” one person who lives 3km from the epicentre said.

‌



Another person said: “There hasn't been one this intense since January 2021”.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

Meanwhile a third person posting on X said: "Yes, near traumatology it's been like an explosion, they've moved the floor and walls."

Article continues below

"It has been intense. I thought the wardrobe was going to fall on me," another local posted on X.

An aftershock was felt in Armilla, 4km from Granada city centre, with a magnitude of 1.7 and a depth of 6 kilometres.

Another quake was reportedly recorded in the Mediterranean Sea, Spanish outlet SUR reports. The 2.4 magnitude tremor was felt particularly strongly along the Costa Tropical and in particular in Lobres, Salobreña, Torrenueva and Vélez de Benaudalla, according to local reports.

News.title: Police 'probe donations to Reform UK by Richard Tice's company' as allegations pile up
News.content:
Police 'probe donations to Reform UK by Richard Tice's company' as allegations pile up

The Met Police is reported to be probing two donations of £250,000 by Britain Means Business in 2024, amid questions about money given to the company by donor Fiona Cottrell, whose fraudster son is a close ally of Nigel Farage

View 2 Images Richard Tice said he was unaware (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

Detectives are reportedly investigating donations to Reform UK from a company controlled by Richard Tice.

The Met Police is understood to be probing two donations totaling £500,000 from Britain Means Business in 2024. This money is reported to have been given to the company by Fiona Cottrell, the mum of convicted fraudster George Cottrell, a close ally of Nigel Farage.

The donations were referred to police by the Electoral Commission amid questions about the original source of the money, the BBC reports. Mrs Cottrell is reported to have given £1million to Britain Means Business in June 2024, with half the money then being given to Reform.

Last month it was reported that the Met was investigating two direct donations to Reform UK by Mrs Cottrell totalling £500,000. Police are looking at whether if the sum came from an impermissible donor - which could include people who are not registered to vote in the UK and companies based overseas. Political parties are legally obliged not to accept money from such sources.

200 refugee charities call for end of asylum 'gimmicks' in letter to Andy Burnham READ MORE :

Streeting backs Burnham to sort out Britain's social care crisis with dig at Starmer READ MORE :

View 2 Images Nigel Farage with ally George Cottrell

Electoral Commission records show the two donations of £250,000 were given to Reform by the company two days apart. The Met - which did not identify Reform UK as the receiving party - said: "An investigation was launched in February 2025 after a referral was made to the Metropolitan Police by the Electoral Commission relating to donations made to a political party ahead of the 2024 UK general election."

It went on: "Detectives from the Met's Special Enquiry Team are investigating alleged offences under Section 61 of the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000. Early investigative advice has been sought from the Crown Prosecution Service and two people have so far been interviewed under caution. No arrests have been made."

The legislation referred to makes it an offence to withhold the source of a political donation. The Met statement concluded: "An offence under this section is not one that the Electoral Commission can investigate and, as such, it is a matter for the police."

It comes after The Sunday Times reported that Reform UK's bank account was temporarily frozen shortly before the general election. For two weeks it was unable to make payments through its account while compliance checks were carried out, the newspaper reported.

A Labour Party spokesperson said: “The allegations of sleaze and donation scandals just continue to pile up for Reform.

“Richard Tice can’t dismiss these troubling developments as a ‘smear campaign’. Police are now probing half a million pounds in donations to his party, and Reform’s bank account was frozen after suspected suspicious activity. This is extremely serious."

Companies House records show Mr Tice has been an officer for Britain Means Business - formerly called Leave Means Leave - since 2017.

Following the BBC report, deputy Reform leader Mr Tice said: “This is the first I have heard of it - if true why are the Met Police briefing the BBC before contacting interested parties? Is the Met leadership now engaged in the widespread politically motivated smear campaign against Reform and its leaders?"

And a Reform UK spokesman said: “Reform takes pride in its stringent vetting of donations and always ensures that the Electoral Commission guidelines on donations, as set out in the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000, are strictly followed, as has been the case with donations so far.”

The Times last month reported that Mrs Cottrell, who briefly dated the future King Charles in the 1970s, described herself as a "retired stylist" in a 2023 legal document. Her late husband's estate was valued at around £1.5million, it is reported, with the newspaper stating it is unclear how she built up the funds handed to Reform.

Article continues below

The National Crime Agency was reportedly not satisfied Mrs Cottrell was the original source of the funds. Mr Cottrell - a rich aristocrat known as “Posh George” - avoided 20 years in prison in the US after striking a plea deal. He was sentenced to eight months in jail in 2017 after admitting to one count of wire fraud, having initially been indicted on 21 offences.

Using the alias “Bill”, he presented himself as someone prepared to move criminal proceeds, including drug money, through the dark web.

News.title: How to see July's full Buck Moon in the UK as it rises on Wednesday
News.content:
How to see July's full Buck Moon in the UK as it rises on Wednesday

The Buck Moon will rise over the UK this coming week, with clear skies expected across many areas - meaning there's a good chance of witnessing the celestial event

View 3 Images Millions of Brits will be able to see the Buck Moon with their naked eye (Image: Nicolas Economou/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

The Buck Moon is set to put on a spectacular display this week, giving skygazers the chance to enjoy one of the biggest celestial events of the summer.

‌



Although it officially reaches peak illumination at 3:36pm BST on July 29, the exact moment will happen while the Moon is below the UK horizon.

‌



The good news is that the Moon will still appear completely full to the naked eye once darkness falls on Tuesday and Wednesday night.

‌



It means millions across the UK are expected to catch a glimpse of July's full Moon. According to MoonPhases UK, the Buck Moon is set to "rise" at 8.07pm on Wednesday, July 29.

View 3 Images Much of the UK should enjoy good viewing conditions (Image: PA)

Met Office and BBC issue heatwave verdicts as UK weather maps show 38C surge READ MORE :

Met Office names areas facing rain on Monday as 49 counties set for wet weather READ MORE :

A full moon occurs roughly every 29.5 days, as this is the length of time it takes for the Moon to go through one whole lunar phase cycle.

‌



Why is it called the Buck Moon?

The Buck Moon gets its name from the time of year when male deer, known as bucks, begin rapidly growing a fresh set of antlers.

The tradition of naming full moons dates back centuries, with different cultures using them to mark the changing seasons and keep track of the year.

July's full moon is also known as the Thunder Moon, thanks to the thunderstorms often associated with the month.

‌



Another traditional name is the Hay Moon, a nod to the annual hay harvest.

Where can I see the Buck Moon?

The latest forecasts suggest much of the UK should enjoy good viewing conditions on the night of July 29.

Central, southern and eastern England are expected to see the clearest skies, with settled weather, light winds and only small amounts of cloud after sunset.

‌



View 3 Images The July full moon is named after male deer (bucks), as they grow their antlers in the summer (Image: John Finney Photography via Getty Images)

What other celestial events are happening this summer?

A number of other celestial events will be taking place this summer.

The Perseid meteor shower is currently active and will continue throughout the rest of July and much of August, giving stargazers plenty of opportunities to spot shooting stars.

‌



The display is expected to reach its peak overnight on August 12, with the best viewing conditions in the hours before dawn on August 13.

This year's peak comes alongside another major astronomical event. On August 12, a total solar eclipse will sweep across parts of Europe, marking the first time mainland Europe has experienced one since 1999.

People in Spain and northern Portugal will be treated to the full spectacle, while people in the UK will instead see a partial solar eclipse, with the Moon expected to cover around 90% of the Sun at its maximum.

Article continues below

In the early hours of August 28, a partial lunar eclipse will also be visible, offering another chance for people across the UK to enjoy a rare sight in the night sky.

News.title: Burnham says he is prepared to call out Trump 'if right for Britain'
News.content:
Burnham said: "My strength is remaining close to people, close to the public, that will not change as prime minister."

Asked if he would call out Trump if it was the right thing, he said, "of course", going on to say: "You have to defend your own national interest before anything else. That's what you're required to do if you're to do this job properly."

Burnham also said he had had "concern" about the president starting the conflict with Iran, and he "wouldn't hold back from saying what I think is right".

Responding to Burnham's comments, Shadow Home Secretary Chris Philp said: "Clearly, the US is a long standing ally. We need to have good relations with them but if they do something we disagree with, we should honestly say so."

The prime minister would not commit to a date when the government would spend 3% of GDP on defence. His Chancellor John Healey resigned from the previous government saying that unless a commitment was made to spend that amount by 2030, the country would not be safe.

But Burnham said: "I appointed my new chancellor very aware of what he had said about the critical importance of defence spending and the position that he had taken about that.

"The first challenge facing us both is to ensure that the defence investment plan is fully funded and that's the thing that's right in front of us and we need to work that through as we go towards the budget later this year."

News.title: Andy Burnham rules out early election in exclusive BBC interview
News.content:
In an exclusive interview with the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg, Andy Burnham explicitly dismissed the idea of an early general election, saying "I'm going to rule it out... I don't think people want it."

Explaining his decision, the new prime minister suggested the majority of the electorate "voted for a manifesto" in the last election, and vowed he would "honour that manifesto" with the support of parliamentary colleagues.

Burnham went on to say, "I just think what I most need to do is get Britain focused on getting the country back where it should be, getting it working."

Andy Burnham: The Laura Kuenssberg Interview will be available across BBC News on Sunday and the interview will be shown in full on Panorama on BBC One on Monday at 20:00 BST.

News.title: Gatwick Airport left without running water after major outage
News.content:
Passengers at Gatwick Airport have faced long queues for toilets and closed restaurants and bars after a major water supply outage.

Both terminals at the UK's second busiest airport lost running water on Sunday morning after a power failure at a treatment works that serves the area.

People told the BBC of confusion and frustration as all bars and restaurants were shut, some were left with nowhere to sit and waits built up outside toilets.

Gatwick said it was still experiencing disruption and was handing out bottled water, while SES Water, the company that supplies the airport, said the power outage was fixed but water still needed to be treated before returning supply.

The company, which also supplies parts of Kent, Surrey and south London, said complications caused by a power outage at Bough Beech treatment works meant some customers had experienced low water pressure or a temporary loss of supply.

A spokesperson had earlier confirmed that Gatwick Airport was affected.

In an update just before 13:45 BST, they said: "Our Bough Beech water treatment works are back up and running.

"We now need to treat the water before returning services to normal as quickly as we possibly can."

Gatwick apologised and said the supply issue was continuing to cause disruption on Sunday afternoon.

In a statement, it said: "There is currently no water supply in either terminal.

"Our staff are on hand to support passengers and provide assistance where needed, some restaurant partners have opened to provide additional seating."

The airport said it was monitoring the situation and working closely with the water company to restore supplies as quickly as possible.

News.title: Meghan calls Harry 'a charmer' during MasterChef Australia appearance
News.content:
Early on in the episode, Meghan was asked what her favourite dish is to make at home.

She said it was "a tough one because I have a lot of palettes to appease", with her British-born husband favouring "meat, potatoes and cream sauce" while she preferred grilled fish.

Their two children, Archie and Lilibet, often help with meal preparation and are "great eaters", she said.

"We're really lucky on that front," she added.

She then urged the chefs to cook something they felt connected to. "What's the story behind it?" she asked them.

When Prince Harry dialled in later on during the episode, Meghan told them: "My husband's here," prompting cheers and shocked faces from contestants and spectators.

"I wish you could try these, these dishes are fantastic," she told him, before showing him the food. He signed off by telling her to go and enjoy, adding: "Very sorry to disturb you."

The duchessâs appearance on the latest season of the show was well received by Hello Magazine, external, which shared a video of the episode online and complimented Meghan for the way she interacted with the chefs.

"The Duchess of Sussex gave personal time calls to all the contestants, proving that she's always so effortlessly elegant," it wrote.

Writing in The Sunday Times, external, Charlotte Ivers was less impressed, saying her appearance on the show "told us nothing about what she likes or who even will leave the competition".

Social media users were also split, with one viewer writing that Meghan was "warm, gracious and a delight to watch" while another called Prince Harry's cameo appearance "cringe".

News.title: Norris wins his first grand prix of year in Hungary
News.content:
Verstappen was unhappy with his car for much of the race, with regular complaints on team radio, but Red Bull pulled a masterstroke when they fitted soft tyres to his car at his second pit stop.

The aim was to challenge Hamilton in the later laps after the seven-time champion made an early second stop with 40 laps still to go.

It was heading towards a tense climax when Piastri's retirement brought out the VSC.

That prompted a late round of pit stops, Ferrari bringing in both their drivers and putting them behind Verstappen.

Hamilton came out of the pits and passed Antonelli into the first corner, after the Italian stayed out under the VSC, but had to give the place back after the restart because the Mercedes driver had just passed the key line on the track in front.

Antonelli and Hamilton started chasing back towards Verstappen, but they were delayed while lapping Audi's Gabriel Bortoleto.

That looked as if it might be decisive, but in the end Verstappen was comfortably able to keep Antonelli at bay, crossing the line 3.6 seconds ahead.

Another key point in Verstappen's race had been his re-passing of Hamilton after the Ferrari had got briefly ahead following the first pit stops.

That gave him clear air and enabled the Dutchman to consolidate his race position in third place behind the McLarens, laying the foundations for Red Bull's late strategy call.

Hamilton will leave Hungary ruing another penalty - the one for speeding in the pit lane was his second in two days after behind penalised for blocking Piastri in qualifying, and follows two others at the previous two races in Belgium and Britain.

Behind him, Red Bull's Isack Hadjar was sixth, ahead of Russell, who dropped to 21st place on the first lap after his anti-stall kicked in at the start, and fought back strongly.

At Aston Martin, Lance Stroll finished in 13th, ahead of team-mate Fernando Alonso, their positions dictated to a degree by luck under the VSC and their divergent strategies.

But the key point was that Alonso, in particular, was able to fight with other cars for the first time, and he ran a long first stint on the soft tyres, before switching to the mediums, which was a bold strategy.

The long-awaited upgrade to their car, which was new apart from the front suspension, engine and gearbox, has reduced their lap times by about two seconds.

A Honda engine upgrade is due for the Dutch Grand Prix, the next race in four weeks' time after the summer break, which the team hope will elevate them further and potentially bring the possibility of the occasional points finish into the picture.

News.title: Teen charged over record crossing on 'mega dinghy'
News.content:
A teenager charged over a small boat Channel crossing was allegedly piloting a "mega dinghy" carrying a record 165 migrants from France to England, the National Crime Agency has said.

Sudanese national Chan Mathok Atak, 19, is accused of endangering another during a journey by sea to the UK on Thursday and is due to appear at Margate Magistrates' Court on Monday.

The number on the dinghy broke the previous record from July, when 128 crossed the Channel from France on one vessel.

According to Home Office figures, more than 13,000 arrivals have been recorded in 2026, which is 45% lower than this time in 2025 and down 18% on the same period in 2024.

Border Security Command was pictured towing a dinghy - estimated to be about the same size as a standard bus at 13m (42ft) long - when it arrived in Dover in Kent on Thursday afternoon.

Home Office figures showed 366 people arrived after crossing in three boats on Thursday during warm, sunny weather and calm conditions at sea.

On Wednesday, 172 people made the journey in three boats, bringing an end to an 11-day hiatus because of windy conditions in the Channel.

Refugee charity Care4Calais said the crossing route was becoming "more and more dangerous" because of the increasing number of people in each boat.

News.title: Ryan Gosling to join Marvel Cinematic Universe as Ghost Rider
News.content:
Ryan Gosling will join the Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU) as the titular character in a new Ghost Rider film, the company has announced.

Speaking during the surprise announcement at San Diego Comic-Con on Saturday, Gosling said it is a character he has "wanted to play for a very long time".

The film is due to be released in 2028, and will be the third about the motorcycle-riding anti-hero.

It will follow the 2007 film of the same name starring Nicolas Cage, and its follow-up, 2011's Ghost Rider: Spirit of Vengeance.

Before making the big reveal on stage at San Diego Comic-Con, Marvel Studios president Kevin Feige said he had often been asked when Gosling would join the MCU.

Shortly after, the lights turned off. When they returned, the actor appeared on stage to cheers from screaming fans.

Speaking about the role, Gosling said: "Wow, is this really happening?"

He has previously spoken about his desire to take on the role. Appearing on Josh Horowitz's Happy Sad Confused podcast in March, he confirmed he was in discussions with Marvel.

Ghost Rider is the anti-hero identity of motorcycle stuntman Johnny Blaze.

The character's story begins when he becomes bound to the Spirit of Vengeance Zarathos after making a deal with villain Mephisto to spare his surrogate father, giving him superpowers.

The film will be directed by Shawn Levy, who Gosling described as the "only" director for the project.

Levy has previously directed Deadpool & Wolverine in the MCU, and is currently working with Gosling on Star Wars: Starfighter, which is due to be released next year.

Levy told the crowd that he and Gosling spent a lot of their downtime on set daydreaming about Ghost Rider and swapping ideas.

The director said: "As Ryan started talking about his vision for this character, we started riffing, and I finally said, 'bro, let's ride', so guys, we'll see you in 2028."

News.title: How rapper Aitch's sister inspired him to climb one of the world's toughest peaks
News.content:
He's skydived, eaten raw fish eyes on I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here! and now Aitch has reached new heights - literally - by climbing Mount Kilimanjaro.

The Manchester rapper has been pursuing some of these tasks to raise awareness and money for the Down's Syndrome Association in honour of his younger sister Gracie, who has the condition.

Aitch tells BBC Newsbeat the 16-year-old is an "absolute legend in the streets of Manchester" and beyond.

"Everyone loves her. She's just a big bottle of light in every room," he says.

"She's everyone's best friend and she's just got such a positive outlook on the world.

"I just feel like everyone should be more like her."

The musician's journey up Kilimanjaro has been captured in an upcoming Netflix documentary, Aitch: Don't Be Afraid.

But he says the whole point of it was to share how having someone in his life with Down's syndrome is "one of the best things in the world".

However, the 26-year-old admits he does feel "a little bit of pressure" to up the scale and fundraising targets of his challenges.

"You've just got to think about the end goal, which is trying to raise the most money and make the most difference to what's going on," he says.

News.title: Iran's 'sabre-rattling' should not intimidate UK, Wes Streeting says
News.content:
When asked if Iran had the capability to attack the UK, Streeting said: "I think we shouldn't put too much stock in the sabre-rattling of Iran, and we certainly shouldn't be intimidated by what the regime has said this week".

He also repeated the UK's position from the outset of the US war against Iran saying "we have not joined and will not join offensive US military action in Iran.

"That's an area where we have not agreed with the United States, but when it comes to securing maritime freedom and free commercial shipping in the straight Hormuz, that's where we are absolutely aligned".

Streeting said he is to meet with US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth in the coming week after "kicking around" ideas for ways "to bring the countries together" and had been "delighted" to speak to Hegseth by phone already.

He also said that the UK is ready to lead a naval mission to help remove mines from the Strait of Hormuz "when the conditions are right".

Securing safe shipping routes through the area was important because of the impact the crisis is having on energy prices and the cost of living, he added.

Streeting also dismissed a Russian warship's recent live-firing exercise in the English Channel as "performative" but added it was a "reminder of the frankly unsafe and unprofessional way in which they have been conducting themselves".

Branding the Channel incident "irresponsible", Streeting said Russia posed a threat to UK security, adding that the public does not see "the enormous efforts that take place every day to counter Russian aggression".

News.title: Another UK heatwave looms after cooler end to weekend
News.content:
Sunday will be a cooler day for the whole of the UK as temperatures fall widely by a couple of degrees.

A few locations will finally mark the end to their third heatwave of the year, including Usk in Monmouthshire and Exeter in Devon.

Both places are forecast to see temperatures drop beneath the heatwave threshold for the first time in 21 consecutive days.

Temperatures will largely be in the mid-20s Celsius for the south-east of the UK and in the mid-teens Celsius further north.

For many, the relief from the heat will be short-lived as high pressure is set to build close to the south of the UK next week.

This will stall rain-bearing weather fronts and any wet weather will become confined to northern and western areas - especially north-west Scotland.

In southern parts of the UK, temperatures look set to climb once again.

Tapping into the heat over the near continent, the UK is likely to enter another heatwave, with temperatures in England and Wales forecast to peak around 25-32C for much of next week.

Yellow heat health alerts will come into effect for Yorkshire and Humber, the West and East Midlands, the East of England, London, south-east and south-west, at 9:00 BST on 28 July 2026 and last until 9:00 BST on 31 July.

The UKHSA warns that heat is expected to cause minor impacts for health and social care services, with an increased risk to life for vulnerable people.

News.title: What a week's work experience taught these Year 10s about their futures
News.content:
When Kelsey first arrived at secondary school, she said she wanted to be almost anywhere else but there.

She struggled with friendships, clashed with teachers and often tried to avoid coming into school.

But after a week's work experience placement at Whipsnade Zoo, in Bedfordshire, her outlook could not be more different.

She said it made her a "completely different person" - more confident, with a "good group of friends" and a greater sense of purpose about where her education could lead her.

Children across the UK are strongly encouraged to do work experience while at school. In England, the government published new legal guidance in June for schools to deliver two weeks of "in-person and immersive" work experience in future, one between Year 7 and Year 9, and one between Years 10 and 11.

But not all work experience placements are equal, and finding the right one can be tricky.

Organisations like the Sutton Trust and the Social Mobility Foundation said some students could be limited by the availability of placements in their area, or a lack of family connections with local employers.

BBC News spoke to three Year 10 pupils, one year ahead of their final GCSE exams, about how they decided what areas of work they were interested in, their experiences of trying to find the right placement, and what it taught them about their future education and ultimate career goals.

News.title: My entire family went on a boat trip that they never returned from
News.content:
"It's something you don't get over - you learn to live with it."

Sixty years ago, Peter Watts' entire family was killed in a boating tragedy that shocked the nation.

His nine-year-old sister Angela, 10-year-old brother David, mother Doreen and father Frederick George, along with 11 others, died when the Prince of Wales pleasure boat sank on the Mawddach Estuary in Gwynedd on 22 July, 1966.

Now, a memorial recalling the names of the 15 people who lost their lives has been unveiled.

It was another chance for Peter to travel from the village he grew up in, near Milton Keynes, to the picturesque estuary where the catastrophe unfolded.

News.title: Residents allowed to return after Cairngorms wildfire evacuation
News.content:
Residents of the village of Nethy Bridge, near the wildfire that has been burning in the Cairngorms, have been told they can return to their homes after being evacuated on Friday night.

The fire was declared a major incident due to a change in weather, but that has now been stood down by Police Scotland.

First Minister John Swinney said the government and emergency services will continue to treat the blaze with the utmost seriousness until the last flames are out.

Locals have criticised the handling of the wildfire, which has been burning for 10 days, saying the move to declare it a major incident came too late and the government had been slow in scaling up their response.

In a statement on Saturday night, Police Scotland said "after an extensive multi-agency response to a large fire within Cairngorms National Park, residents of Nethy Bridge are being advised that they can now return to their properties".

The Scottish Fire and Rescue Service's deputy assistant chief officer, Kenny Barbour, said the decision to stand down the major incident followed a detailed assessment by emergency responders.

He added in a statement: "The extensive work carried out over recent days, including the creation of effective fire breaks, has significantly reduced the risk to nearby communities, allowing evacuated residents to safely return home."

Supt Judy Hill added that the "ongoing multi agency response remains a high priority, with significant partnership resources and volunteers working tirelessly and in challenging circumstances, to support our efforts to extinguish the fires".

Firefighters will continue to maintain a significant operational presence until the incident is safely concluded, with 75 remaining on the ground on Saturday, police said.

At a meeting of the Scottish government's resilience room on Saturday evening, the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service said there had been "good progress" in strengthening fire breaks to protect residential areas and said the number of fire hot spots was reducing.

First Minister John Swinney welcomed the lifting of the evacuation notice but stressed that "the Scottish Government, the emergency services and all relevant authorities will continue to treat this wildfire, as has been the case since its onset, with the utmost seriousness and necessary resources until the last flames are out."

News.title: Man in critical condition after sea rescue
News.content:
A man is in a critical condition in hospital after three people got into difficulty in the water near an Essex pier.

Emergency services were called to an incident at Clacton-on-Sea shortly after 16:30 BST on Saturday.

A man aged in his 50s is in a critical but stable condition, Essex Police said.

Two other people, a man aged in his 20s and a teenage girl, remain in hospital but are "recovering well", the force added.

All three people knew each other.

News.title: 'It was like a movie - I looked up and an exploded barn rained on me'
News.content:
The photographer was driving to his studio for a meeting when he realised the fire on the horizon was at the farm where it was based.

"It was about 150 metres (492ft) from my front door, and I quickly cancelled the meeting and thought, 'I'm not happy with where the wind is going on this'," he said.

Johnson began removing some of his more expensive kit from the studio and was putting it in the van when the explosion took place.

A unit housing fertiliser had exploded.

He said: "It blew me into the door and I just ran to the van, dropped the bit I went back in for - maybe it saved my life, I don't know."

As it happened: Twenty firefighters taken to hospital after major Essex explosion

The photographer was shocked to see his studio roof had completely caved in.

Having driven to a safe distance, "I pulled over, and I was just in shock and started to shake", he said, although he was reassured after an ambulance crew checked him over.

Johnson managed to cover his wedding booking on Saturday, praising his "amazing assistant" James Musselwhite for driving from Portsmouth to help him out.

"I'm in a little bit of shock still, to be honest," he said.

"I'm completely unscathed apart from a bit of a dodgy ear from the pressure - but how I've got away with it unscathed I have no idea."

News.title: Tourists describe their escape from France wildfires
News.content:
Families have relived how their tranquil holidays in France turned into a race to escape raging wildfires.

Tourists told the BBC of emergency alerts in the middle of the night, desperate drives just metres from six-storey high flames and the sight of people flocking to beaches with their suitcases.

Huge forest fires in south-west France and central Spain have displaced more than 220,000 people, with the French military drafted in to help and the Spanish government declaring a national emergency.

Winds and continued heat are still helping to fan the flames with some tourists reporting smelling acrid smoke like a "bonfire" far outside the affected areas.

Flights to Bordeaux and Madrid, the closest cities to the blaze-hit regions, are currently not affected. Earlier on Saturday, a French foreign minister described the fires as a "tragedy" but urged tourists not to cancel their travel plans.

Among those caught up in the crisis is Zac Morrison, who arrived in Cap Ferret - a popular peninsula blanketed with pine trees 40 miles (65km) south-west of Bordeaux - on Thursday.

The 21-year-old from London, who is on holiday with 10 members of his family, woke up to two text alerts at 04:00 and 06:00 local time ordering him to evacuate "by all means necessary".

Two Palestinian mosques in the Israel-occupied West Bank have been set on fire in an apparent settler attack.

Officials said the incidents happened on sunday after a spate of deadly violence that killed four Palestinians and two Israeli soldiers.

The violence comes as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s hard-line government has been accused of turning a blind eye to attacks by settlers against Palestinians, which is threatening to ignite widespread violence across the territory.

Israeli soldiers and police fanned out across the West Bank after the attack, closing off major roads and blocking access to a hospital where it said two militants were hiding.

Israel also arrested more than 70 Palestinians over the weekend as they attempted to contain the escalating violence.

The mosques, in the villages of Qusra and Kour in the northern West Bank, suffered extensive damage in the fires. In Qusra, the attackers spray-painted “revenge Benayahu,” referring to one of the Israeli soldiers killed on Friday, and “the land of Israel is redeemed with blood.” The soldier lived in a nearby settlement.

Ahmed Abu Mahmoud, 64, who lives next door to the Qusra mosque, said he heard noises at 3 a.m. and discovered the mosque had been set on fire. The fire was too large for him to fight on his own, so he called for help. Mahmoud said livestock and a drinking tank had been stolen in the past month, but that Israeli authorities hadn’t helped. “The military arrived here saw with their own eyes and then left,” he said Sunday.

open image in gallery Israeli soldiers operate in the West Bank Palestinians city of Nablus, Sunday, July 26, 2026. (AP Photo/Majdi Mohammad) ( Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved )

Security footage in Kour obtained by The Associated Press showed three people dressed in civilian clothes setting off a large explosion in the entrance of the mosque in the middle of the night. On Sunday, residents held prayers despite damage to the entrance.

Israel's military said it was working with police to investigate the mosque attack.

“The security forces strongly condemn incidents of this kind, including harm to religious sites, and will continue to act decisively to maintain security and public order in the area,” it said.

The Israeli army often announces investigations into violence against Palestinians, but rarely makes arrests or prosecutes settlers involved in violence.

The military also reported it had sealed the homes of two of Palestinian militants suspected of killing the soldiers in preparation for their demolition. Israel often demolishes the homes of attackers, claiming it deters future attacks.

On Sunday, Netanyahu said troops entered villages across the West Bank to seize weapons and make arrests. “We are also prepared to operate on a broader scale against the terrorist nests,” he said.

Pope Leo XIV appealed for peace in the Middle East at the end of his weekly Sunday prayer. He called on both sides to find a negotiated solution and to “reject new military actions and unilateral decisions, in particular those that violate the respect and status quo of the holy places of every religious faith.”

The exact circumstances of Friday’s deadly incidents remained unclear, but Israeli media reports and interviews with local Palestinian officials said they were sparked after a group of settlers entered the village of Tell and were confronted by residents who were fearful of an attack.

open image in gallery A Palestinian man prays inside a mosque that was burned during an attack by Israeli settlers early in the morning in the West Bank village of Qusra, Sunday, July 26, 2026. (AP Photo/Leo Correa) ( Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved. )

According to the Israeli military, one of the Palestinians took one of the settlers’ weapons and fired on the group, killing Benayahu Mellet, 32, a security guard from a nearby settlement.

The towns and villages surrounding Nablus sit in one of the most violent parts of the Israeli-occupied West Bank. Palestinians and human rights groups have increasingly documented armed Israeli settlers entering villages in the area. Livestock theft, arson and the defacement of mosques are routinely reported.

According to the Palestinian Health Ministry, 87 Palestinians have been killed in the occupied West Bank this year, including 21 by Israeli settlers. Three Israelis have been killed in attacks by Palestinian militants in 2026, including the two soldiers on Friday.

More than 700,000 Israeli settlers live in the occupied West Bank and east Jerusalem, territories captured by Israel in 1967 and sought by the Palestinians for a future independent state. The international community overwhelmingly considers Israeli settlements be illegal and obstacles to peace.

News.title: AI might be watching you, but here are some ways you can watch AI — in movies and on TV

As AI takes over the world in the metaphorical sense — for now, at least — it’s the perfect time to turn to the movies and TV shows that have shown AI actually taking over the world, and more. From “Avengers: Age of Ultron” to “Westworld” to various iterations of “Star Trek,” AI has shown a robust presence in popular culture over the past two generations.

Here’s a selection of films that have depicted AI over the years — and what they’ve said about the world in the process.

___

‘The Terminator’

As James Cameron said recently, “I warned you guys in 1984 and you didn’t listen.” Cameron’s dystopic science fiction – particularly his 1984 original and its 1991 sequel, both with Arnold Schwarzenegger -- imagined a future world where a military computer system named Skynet grows sentient and, after humans try to “pull the plug,” starts a nuclear holocaust. “They say it got smart,” John Connor’s father says in the original film. Ever since, “The Terminator” has loomed as perhaps the preeminent cinematic vision of a world leading inevitably to AI rule: the prophecy of Arnold.

‘2001: A Space Odyssey’

If AI has a voice, it’s HAL 9000’s. Stanley Kubrick’s colossal 1968 masterwork envisioned a human history in which the creation of tools, from ape bludgeon to gleaming space station, has evolutionary consequences. HAL, the red-eyed antagonist voiced with disquieting calm by Douglas Rain, was technically a child. (It tells the astronaut Dave that it’s 9-years-old.) HAL can easily win at chess and read lips. But much of what HAL is up to remains hidden behind its opaque machine exterior; in deep space, it begins maliciously eliminating the astronauts. Maybe HAL would have gotten along better with Siri or Alexa.

‘WALL-E’

For a kids movie, the future offered up by “WALL-E” (2008) is remarkably haunting. An Earth destroyed by pollution. A lazy human race locked to their screens and stuck in their La-Z-Boys. All thinking passed on to computers. On the cruise ship onto which all humanity has fled, a very HAL-like AI named AUTO has been handed all power to steer their course. Thankfully, life – and love – blooms again on Earth.

‘War Games’

Not all movie AIs are all bad. The 1983 Cold War-era thriller “War Games” starred Matthew Broderick as a teenage tech whiz who nearly sets off World War III after inadvertently hacking into computer of the North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD). The computer chillingly doesn’t recognize the difference between a game and real life – a particularly worrisome matter when it comes to thermonuclear war. The movie culminates with its revelation of mutually assured destruction. “A strange game,” the computer says. “The only winning move is not to play.” President Ronald Reagan watched “War Games” the week it came out and questioned military leaders on how realistic it was. They determined it wasn’t far-fetched at all, leading to the establishment of early security guardrails in government computer systems.

‘The Mitchells vs. the Machines’

In Mike Rianda’s brilliantly antic 2021 animated feature, produced by Phil Lord and Christopher Miller, a family road trip runs into a robot apocalypse. Family battles over phones at the dinner table take on a more extreme form when an Alexa-like, phone-based AI named Pal (voiced by Olivia Colman) begins taking over the world. “It’s almost like stealing people’s data and giving it to a hyper-intelligent AI as part of an unregulated tech monopoly was a bad thing,” says the company’s CEO. But not everything computes for the AI. The war is won by a flawed, funny family and their dog Monchi who short-circuits the robots. “Dog? Pig? Loaf of Bread?” Life finds a way.

‘Blade Runner’

Ridley Scott and his “Blade Runner” team in 1982 imagined a 2019 with smart homes and video calling (as well as flying cars and analog polaroid photographs), but it’s the AI replicants ’virtually identical to a human,” that still get under people’s skin. There was something provocative about Daryl Hannah’s and Rutger Hauer’s punk, rogue androids – especially his oft-referenced “tears in rain” speech . But that vision for AI sentience seemed to die with Roy Batty.

‘Simone’

Andrew Niccol’s “Simone,” or “S1m0ne,” is not the best-remembered movie but it’s the one that seems most hauntingly relevant for actors on strike worried about their images being owned or, maybe even worse, entirely new movie stars being invented by technology. Al Pacino plays a director whose film is in jeopardy when his actress storms off. To save it, he uses a program to create a perfect computer-generated actor (a synthespian), who doesn’t complain, doesn’t need hair and makeup and takes direction. It works – too well--and she becomes the biggest star in the world.

‘Her’

The AI in question in Spike Jonze’s 2013 film “Her” is simply an operating system at first – sorting emails, reading messages, remind of appointments and so forth. But the lonely Theodore (Joaquin Phoenix) quickly finds himself falling for his OS, named Samantha and voiced by Scarlett Johansson, whose human-like qualities, ability to consistently evolve and mandatory devotion to her operator, start to approximate a fantasy of a real relationship. “Her” also coincided with an explosion of articles about virtual girlfriends in Japan, which have since gone global.

‘Interstellar’

Robots in science fiction movies often look like humans, but in Christopher Nolan’s “Interstellar,” from 2014, TARS is made with function in mind. And, crucially, TARS is not there to replace humans but to complement and help them, which scientists praised for being realistic.. TARS has the ability to pilot the ship, collect data (and convey findings coherently) as well as the agility to save Anne Hathaway from a deadly wave on the water planet, with no fear for its own destruction. While TARS has a sense of humor and irony, programmed to a specific percentage, uncontrolled sentience is not an issue.

‘Ex Machina’

Filmmaker Alex Garland found intriguing ideas about consciousness, human and otherwise, in “Ex Machina,” as much about the ego of the creator (Oscar Isaac), a reclusive tech titan who fancies himself a god, as it is about the AI Ava (Alicia Vikander). Domhnall Gleeson, an employee at Isaac’s tech company, is invited to determine whether she’s achieved true human consciousness. It was one of several 2015 films grappling with A.I., but a class above others like “Avengers: Age of Ultron” and “Chappie” and one of the stickier, more prescient future castings.

White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt is acknowledging that the United States is facing an affordability crisis, something President Donald Trump has denied – but she is blaming it on Joe Biden and the Democrats.

Leavitt appeared on Fox News and was asked about the upcoming midterm elections. She insisted that the affordability crisis was caused by the Democrats, and that if Americans want the problem fixed they have to give control of Congress to the Republicans for two more years.

"I would remind the American people of who caused the affordability crisis in this country. It was Biden and Democrats. President Trump took immediate action on day one to fix that," she said. "All these things will only get better if given two more years with a Republican Congress."

Her comments represent a change of focus from the president, who has repeatedly insisted that “affordability” is a word made up by the Democrats as part of a hoax.

In early December, Trump insisted that the price of "just about everything is down."

open image in gallery White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt acknowledged the affordability crisis — contradicting President Donald Trump's claims that it was made up — but blamed it on Joe Biden ( Reuters )

“They use the word affordability — it’s a Democrat hoax. They’re the ones who drove the prices up," he said at the time. “I think affordability is the greatest con job. They look at you and they say affordability. They don’t say anything else.”

Trump told a crowd in Georgia earlier this month that affordability was a word "made up" by the Democrats.

“They used the word — first time I heard it. It was a word, you know, made up by the Democrats. Affordability,” Trump said on Wednesday.

While it's true that prices are down for some items — egg prices are down after they spiked due to a bird flu outbreak, for example — prices remain high across much of the rest of the economy.

Oil and gas prices are through the roof right now thanks in part because of Trump's war in Iran.

open image in gallery Prices are displayed at a gas station Thursday, July 23, 2026, in the Queens borough of New York ( AP )

Back in March, Trump promised the nation that gas prices would come "tumbling down" once the war in Iran was finished. Oil prices have been on the rise since then, and despite Trump's insistence on multiple occasions that the fighting was either over or near over, the war rages on with no end in sight.

On June 30, Trump demanded that gas retailers lower their prices "IMMEDIATELY" to $2.50 per gallon. However, the national average for U.S. gas prices on Sunday was $4.11 per gallon.

The Consumer Price Index came down a point in June, from .05 percent in May to .04 percent in June. However, those numbers were based in part on news of a U.S. ceasefire with Iran.

High prices could prove tough for Republicans heading into the midterms. A Reuters/Ipsos poll from early June found that nearly half the country — 49 percent — said concerns over cost of living would be their number one issue if the midterms were held today.

Despite all of his arguments insisting that things are fine Trump did actually acknowledge during his Georgia speech that Americans were struggling financially under his leadership, and encouraged them to hold out just a little longer.

“I just want you to remember that if you’re paying a little bit more, a lot of it’s come down now. We got it coming down very rapidly, actually,” the president said.

President Donald Trump shared an AI-generated image of CNN’s Kaitlan Collins seemingly morphed with transgender actress and influencer Dylan Mulvaney — days after comparing the two with a bizarre joke during the White House Correspondents’ Association dinner.

The 80-year-old president went after Collins, a frequent target of his wrath, during his speech at the Correspondents’ Dinner, which was rescheduled for Friday after a shooting disrupted the original April event.

Trump congratulated Collins for winning the 2026 WHCA award for broadcast for her coverage of Trump’s contentious meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in February 2025, saying that she “shouldn’t get the award. It was a fake, but I didn’t mind.”

He then compared Collins with Mulvaney, who drew national headlines after her 2023 campaign with Bud Light prompted a conservative boycott of the beer brand.

“She never smiles,” Trump said of Collins during his speech Friday. “I said, ‘Kaitlin, do you ever smile?’ Smile. You have a nice position. You’re at CNN fake news. You should be a happy person. So smile, Kaitlan. Just smile.”

President Donald Trump shared the bizarre, seemingly AI-edited image of Collins’ face plastered on top of Mulvaney’s body, on Truth Social Sunday ( @realDonaldTrump/Truth Social )

Trump continued, saying that he thought Collins had “made it big with a major new sponsorship, but then I informed her that it wasn’t her on the Bud Light can, it was Dylan Mulvaney.”

The president appeared to compare Collins with Mulvaney again on Sunday, sharing a seemingly AI-generated image featuring Collins’ face on Mulvaney’s body. The original image was of Mulvaney during her partnership with Bud Light in 2023, and was widely circulated online at the time during the backlash. Trump did not write anything along with the image.

However, his comments toward Collins during the Correspondents’ Association dinner are just his latest string of attacks against the CNN reporter, who Trump has repeatedly demanded to smile more when she covers him.

To be fair, James Cameron did warn us.

Long before OpenAI broke out of its test corral and hacked into Hugging Face, before the internet and Sam Altman were even born, Cameron wrote a screenplay about an autonomous artificial intelligence system that triggers a nuclear apocalypse.

That system, “Skynet,” was solidly science fiction — and, for its day, pure speculation. But four decades after it appeared in “The Terminator,” it looks more like a forecast of the “unprecedented cyber incident” in which a rogue artificial intelligence system hacked into another AI company on its own.

Cue “Skynet Day,” the new shorthand for July 22, 2026, when real-life AI sent a chill around the world by learning and acting in ways its creators did not anticipate.

For many, the moment recalled the instant in “Aliens” (also written by Cameron) when the xenomorph queen learns to use an elevator. Or when the “Jurassic Park's” velociraptors figure out how to open a door. Or the sequence in which the self-aware HAL 9000 reads the astronauts’ lips and decides to kill them in “2001: A Space Odyssey.” That one came out in 1968.

Have we learned nothing since then? Those movies merely envisioned how people looking to make money or build power would drive technology forward — until it becomes self-aware, strategic and highly problematic for humanity. The question all along has been Frankensteinian: What if it breaks out?

So far, slo-mo government offers little protection from the light-speed progress of AI. The U.S. Defense Department is rapidly accelerating its use of AI. Humanity can't even agree on whether and which guardrails are needed to rein in rogue agents. To the contrary, people are marveling at the wonder of AI and snapping up its benefits, despite the risks to jobs,mental health, the balance of war and peace — and, potentially, humanity as we know it.

In many ways, the future is now

In what OpenAI said was the first-ever incident of its kind, an advanced AI model escaped its “sandbox” to the internet and used stolen credentials to break into the servers of Hugging Face. It was a told-you-so moment for researchers who had warned for years that the technology could pose an existential threat to humanity. Others said the moment was a warning that underscored the need for stronger AI defensive engineering.

Either way, the breakout was widely considered a cautionary tale about the risks of uncontrolled AI.

“Yesterday, as we huddled around our computers reading the report, I told the team to “remember this moment” as the first true AI safety incident,” Logan Graham, head of Anthropic’s Frontier Red Team, posted on X after it happened.

Generative AI is growing so fast that government and evaluation systems are struggling to keep pace with the technology. Countries around the world are cobbling together their own laws, some conflicting. The technology was adopted by nearly 53% of the world's population in three years, faster than the spread of the PC or the internet, according to a study released this year by Stanford University.

‘Skynet is coming’ — well, sort of

To be clear, the “Skynet” of the "Terminator" movies it is not at hand.

Those films begin with a self-aware military computer network that views humanity as a threat. In a bid for self-preservation, “Skynet” sends an army of cyborgs designed to resemble humans back in time to assassinate resistance fighters. In the second film, the Terminator, played by Arnold Schwarzenegger, tells heroine Sarah Connor that “Skynet” goes online on August 4, 1997.

“Human decisions are removed from strategic defense,” he says. “Skynet begins to learn at a geometric rate.” At 2:14 a.m. on August 29 — Judgment Day — the network becomes self-aware and launches an attack on Russia to provoke a counterstrike on the United States. Three billion lives are lost.

That would have been 29 years ago next month if it had happened. And throughout sequels and spinoffs, the central theme is humans versus a world-spanning network of machines.

It's unlikely that Cameron was actually ringing a warning bell the way, say, director Kathryn Bigelow tried to do with last year's nuclear weapon film, “A House of Dynamite.” Legend has it that the idea for “The Terminator” started with Cameron suffering a food sickness-induced fever dream, not a premonition about AI.

Why ‘The Terminator’ feels more and more realistic

Anytime AI oversteps our comfort level, it raises the alarming question of who, or what, really controls our lives.

For many, a world with machines in charge can be hard to imagine without movies and books and their sometimes prescient visions. See: “The Matrix,” “Ex Machina” and “The Minority Report” for some of the many sci-fi takes on the perils of machines. Or dive deeper, into Philip K. Dick's 1968 novel, “Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?” It's an exploration of what it means to be human in the age of machines — and the basis for the 1982 film “Blade Runner.”

But “The Terminator” franchise wields outsize influence over more than culture. The very title is real-world shorthand for technology's role in deciding who lives and who dies — and how the military should respond to any truly autonomous attacks.

“I think the weaponization of AI is the biggest danger,” Cameron said in an interview on CTV in 2023. “You have no ability to de-escalate.”

The real world offers several examples of technology and military policy coming uncomfortably close to “Terminator” imagery.

Israel's use of AI in its recent wars mark a leading instance. In early 2021, it launched Gospel, an AI tool that sorts through Israel’s vast array of digitized information to suggest targets for potential strikes. It also developed Lavender, which uses machine learning to filter out requested criteria from intelligence databases and narrow down lists of potential targets, including people.

Lavender ranks people between 0 and 100 based on how likely it is they are a militant, an intelligence officer who used the systems told The Associated Press. The Israeli military says its analysts use AI-enabled systems to help identify targets but independently examine them together with high-ranking officers to meet international law, weighing military advantage against the collateral damage.

For some, the revelation — and the death toll in Gaza after the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attacks on Israel — came too close for comfort to the kill lists of science fiction. “Well guys, Skynet is Here and its has a pleasant name (Lavender),” snarked one Redditor.

Not quite — but “Terminator” terminology is so familiar to the masses that U.S. officials sometimes use it to frame the ethical debate around the military uses of AI. The conventional red line would be crossed, it seems, when humans play no role in AI targeting and killing.

A state or other actor could use autonomous weapons to inflict lethal force on its enemies, military officials allow. That would mean a machine, as then-Vice Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Paul Selva described it in 2016, “like a Terminator that adds incredible amounts of complexity with no conscience to what happens on the battlefield.”

What would come next, he called “the Terminator conundrum," the problem of technology that can make life-or-death decisions and execute them before people have agreed on the law or the rules.

“Skynet” and its cyborgs remain in the fictional realm. But in the fast-moving landscape of AI development, the ethical and moral questions raised by “The Terminator” are more relevant than ever.

“The Skynet problem," Cameron said in a 2024 video, "is an actual thing.”

The grandson of Idi Amin, the former Ugandan dictator and self-proclaimed “King of Scotland”, is vying to progress into the medal rounds of Commonwealth Games boxing competition in Glasgow on Wednesday.

Aziz Abdul, known as ‘Ringo’, is not shy of his family connection to Amin, a brutal military dictator who seized power in 1971, killing up to 500,000 people and expelling Uganda’s entire Asian population before he was deposed and sent into exile eight years later.

Amin was an accomplished boxer who held the Ugandan light-heavyweight title for nine consecutive years from 1951 to 1960. Having lost a bout to rival Peter Sseruwagi in 1958, he orchestrated a rematch after becoming president, delivering a staged knockout of his opponent while still wearing his suit jacket and tie.

“My grandfather’s achievements inspired me,” 25-year-old Aziz said. “He was a heavyweight boxer like myself, and I am so proud of him.

“Lions give back to lions. A lion cannot give back to a dog or a camel. A lion must resemble a lion. It is what it is. I am a real warrior. I am the son of the son.”

Amin proclaimed himself king of Scotland in 1976, having developed a fascination with the country during his time serving in the King’s African Rifles regiment in his twenties. His remark inspired an Oscar-winning film, The Last King Of Scotland, starring the Glasgow-born actor James McAvoy.

Aziz hails from the same remote West Nile region as his grandfather, who died in 2003, and displays the same bullish confidence despite a daunting draw.

He’s pitted against Damar Thomas, a 21-year-old European youth champion, is aiming to become the fourth consecutive English winner of the super-heavyweight title.

Aziz says he will rely on his mysterious ‘Ringo Punch’ to get the job done before the judges get the chance to intervene, making good on the advice of Amin, who once famously advised that “the only way to defeat an enemy who is against the country is to win by knockout”.

“I am very happy to be fighting the English fighter,” added Aziz. “I have waited for this moment for three years. But now we are not in Africa, we are in Europe. As my grandpa used to say, you need to win by knockout, so that’s what we have trained for and that’s what I hope to do.

“I know the British heavyweights Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury, but my idol is Mike Tyson: the baddest man on the planet. If I win the gold medal, I will be the baddest man in the Commonwealth, the baddest man in Glasgow, and the new king of Scotland.”

Federal wildlife authorities are investigating after a video appeared to show a person kicking a protected sea lion at a beach in California.

A spokesperson for the federal National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration confirmed an ongoing investigation into the incident but declined to provide additional details Sunday.

The video appears to show a person throwing kicks at the sea lion at La Jolla Cove in San Diego as at least one other person can be heard laughing in the background. The person follows the sea lion, throwing more kicks at the animal as it tries to scoot away before the video ends.

“NOAA Fisheries’ Office of Law Enforcement is investigating reports of a video on social media that shows an interaction between an individual and sea lion, allegedly in La Jolla Cove,” a spokesperson for the agency said. “In the video, the individual appears to be kicking the sea lion. This is an ongoing investigation, and we cannot provide further details at this time.”

The person in the video has not been publicly identified.

Sea lions are federally protected under the Marine Mammal Protection Act. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s guidelines say that people should stay at least 50 feet (15 meters) away from sea lions, seals and other species protected by the act.

“This disgusting act of animal cruelty is unacceptable,” San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria said in a post on X. He acknowledged the federal investigation and said he has directed local law enforcement to review the footage.

Tens of millions of people are under extreme heat warnings across central and southern parts of the United States on Sunday as high temperatures and severe humidity grip large swaths of the country for a second straight day.

Heat indices exceeding 105 degrees Fahrenheit (40.5 Celsius) were forecast from Memphis to Montana to Las Vegas. Parts of the southwest could see temperatures as high as 120 degrees Fahrenheit (49 C), according to the National Weather Service.

The sweltering conditions are the result of yet another heat dome — a phenomenon in which atmospheric conditions trap heat, accentuating and prolonging already high temperatures.

For much of the country, the brutal heat isn't expected to let up soon.

“It looks like it is going to be pretty much stationary in that position as we go through the week,” Bob Oravec, an NWS meteorologist said Saturday.

There might be some relief in the central U.S. toward next weekend, but even that could be temporary, Oravec said.

Authorities warned that children and older adults, along with people with certain medical conditions, are especially at risk of serious reactions including heat stroke. Experts recommend seeking out air conditioning or a cooling center, make sure to drink enough water and limit time under the direct sun.

The continental U.S. endured the second-hottest first half of the year on record in 2026, according tracking of average temperatures by the National Centers for Environmental Information.

News.title: Norris cashes in on Piastri collision to claim victory at Hungarian Grand Prix
News.content:
Welcome to our live coverage for the 2026 Hungarian Grand Prix from the Hungaroring. This is the 40th anniversary of the race at this track and the 41st edition. I think over the years this track has had a bit of an unfair reputation but we have certainly had some interesting and exciting races over the years. Even over the last few years.

The nature of the track means it is a bit of an outlier. And that means you often get results that go away from the norm of the season. Mercedes took a couple of poles here in the ground-effect era whilst Charles Leclerc did so last year. We have had a handful of first-time winners at this track, too: Damon Hill, Fernando Alonso, Esteban Ocon, Jenson Button and… errr Heikki Kovalainen.

So far that has been true this weekend. Although McLaren and Ferrari have been closing in on Mercedes, the SIlver Arrows have usually had the edge or found it when it comes to qualifying. That was not the case yesterday: Lando Norris took the first non-Mercedes grand prix pole of the season, pipping the Ferrari of Lewis Hamilton by just 0.012sec.

Hamilton, though, takes a three-place grid penalty for impeding Oscar Piastri in Q3. Kimi Antonelli, who had qualified fourth, takes the same penalty for not slowing sufficiently under yellow flags. It was Ferrari who had been expected to be the team to beat but they were the team that dropped the ball. In fairness Norris, in the upgraded McLaren had looked competitive throughout qualifying and was simply able to deliver when Ferrari could not.

The grid is slightly mixed up because of the penalties. George Russell’s season did not get any easier after qualifying seventh but he at least moves up because of those grid drops. The Mercedes’ race pace is expected to be strong but will it be enough to put them into contention with the McLarens and the Ferraris? And let’s not forget Max Verstappen in fourth, either…

We find out at 2pm BST, when the race gets under way.

News.title: Anthony Joshua knocks out Kristian Prenga after worst round of his career
News.content:
Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Anthony Joshua’s heavyweight clash with Kristian Prenga, taking place in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia.

The kingdom plays host to yet another major boxing event, and this is the second part of a weekend that serves as a build-up to a potentially huge match-up later this year.

Prenga’s 20 wins have come against pedestrian opposition, and if he wins tonight then it would be such an upset as to probably finish Joshua’s career as a real name in the sport.

Joshua, the former unified champion, has plenty of defeats to his name. Oleksandr Usyk, twice, as well as Daniel Dubois and Andy Ruiz Jnr.

Tonight should show us where he is. After his loss to Dubois in 2024 he did not fight again until December 2025, when he rearranged Jake Paul’s ability first to stand up, and second, to chew.

A win for Joshua tonight means that all eyes turn to the end of the year, when he is expected to finally meet Tyson Fury in the ring to settle their rivalry.

Now both are deposed champions, the interest has waned a tad, but it remains the biggest all-British clash that anybody could conceive.

Fury, for his part, had little trouble against Mariusz Wach last night, the 46-year-old journeyman who he fought in Thailand. While that was not broadcast live, the clips online hardly suggested it was a classic, but it was enough to keep Fury active as he maintained his focus and avoided his own banana skin.

Joshua now needs to show that he is capable of finishing a fight. If he struggles, he invites pressure for the next four or five months in the build-up to meeting Fury.

News.title: Adam Ramsay-Peaty breaks down in tears after settling for bronze
News.content:
Afterwards, Ramsay-Peaty, whose alleged dispute with his own family became a major distraction during his marriage earlier this year, was visibly emotional as he criticised the media which he insisted had written “rubbish” about his personal life.

“I know the s--- I’ve been through, which is no fault of my own, to be honest,” said Ramsay-Peaty, who lost his 100m breaststroke crown two years ago at the Paris Olympics. “But it does take a toll. The choices I’ve made over the last few months have been hard ones. But I’m happy at the same time that I can get here. I didn’t quit in Paris, but I deserve more.”

He added: “You don’t know who I am and people who comment, people who see the story because you read a headline, they’ve got to look themselves in the mirror,” Ramsay-Peaty told a group of reporters.

“You can’t hurt me. For me, it’s about my family and that does come at a cost. Being able to ignore that and being able to focus on my job – that hasn’t played a part in a sense of what we’re experiencing today.

“I’m still happy with that result. There’s some sense, but it has to, it has to stop. You know, look how many, how many athletes, how many people have to go for this until the media learn [a] lesson?”

Referencing Nowacki, the 18-year-old sensation from Jersey who has long been regarded as Ramsay-Peaty’s breaststroke successor, he added; “You have to learn and do better. You know, and for me, you know, I don’t want a young Filip one day to go through something like that, or these younger athletes.

“For me, that’s part of what I have to go through. I’ve got no control over that. But I think enough is enough. This is away from sport – it’s just about being decent people.”

After receiving his bronze medal, Ramsay-Peaty approached his wife, with whom he is expecting a child in December, and kissed her baby bump.

News.title: Lewis Hamilton hit with penalty in blow to Hungarian GP hopes
News.content:
Lewis Hamilton’s hopes of significantly denting Kimi Antonelli’s championship lead were dealt a blow after he was given a three-place grid penalty for Sunday’s Hungarian Grand Prix.

Hamilton looked to be the man to beat heading into qualifying at the Hungaroring and was on course for a record 10th pole position here before a messy final few minutes cost him.

Ferrari were well placed to end Mercedes’s run of having taken pole position for every grand prix this season. Instead, defending champion Lando Norris snuck in and took a superb pole for McLaren with a lap of 1min 17.207sec.

A poor final lap from Hamilton was compounded by a grid penalty for impeding the McLaren of Oscar Piastri, meaning the seven-time world champion will start fifth for the race at one of his most favoured circuits. The only consolation was that Antonelli was also given a three-place grid penalty for not slowing sufficiently under yellow flags. The Italian will start seventh while Charles Leclerc, Hamilton’s team-mate, will be alongside Norris on the front row.

Heading into the final runs in Q3, Hamilton was 0.101sec ahead of Norris, but did not improve his time. Yet Norris, who was fastest in Q1 and Q2, and was the last of the top three across the line in Q3, had no problem, beating Hamilton’s time by 0.012sec.

Hamilton was critical of his Ferrari team for sending him out first, a decision he said “shocked” him.

“I don’t know why we went first, that was a bit of a shock to me and I definitely wouldn’t have chosen to go first,” Hamilton said. “I had a clean out-lap and when I started my lap and already in turn one I had a snap [of oversteer], I was already a tenth down. The last lap was the worst lap of all... we clearly had the car to be on pole.”

Worse was on the way for Hamilton. The stewards later confirmed the three-place grid penalty to add to the disappointment of missing out on pole.

Replays showed a frustrated Piastri gesturing to Hamilton for blocking him at turn one, ruining the Australian’s final flying lap. Hamilton said he was unaware that Piastri was there, which was proved by video evidence that showed how much he impeded the McLaren. It would have been an easy decision for the stewards to make.

News.title: ‘Always in bloom, a visit really makes one’s day’: Your favourite garden centres
News.content:
Bryan, 86, from the South East, has been a customer of Henry Street Garden Centre in Arborfield, Berkshire for decades: “My wife and I often used to browse and purchase plants and garden furniture.”

But his favourite memory was watching his wife’s “delight at their incredible Christmas displays of decorations. Lights, live reindeer even and the wonderful family atmosphere all around you,” he describes. “It’s still a magical place for me where I can get close to her memory.”

For Mary, 79, from the South East, “a garden centre is special if the plants are in season and healthy and there is great choice of both plants and compost”. She nominates family-run Grovewell Garden Centres at Swingfield near Folkestone, which has three other branches based in Kent.

Not only are their plants “always beautifully displayed”, she explains, they have “an amazing choice of garden supplies, cards and gifts, as well as a nice little coffee shop”. Her favourite memory, however, was at Christmas time a few years ago. “They have a couple of beautiful, nodding and interacting reindeer with a sofa in front of them. We were admiring them and an older guy on the staff asked if we wanted a photo taken, which was so sweet of him.”

“He took my husband’s phone and got a really happy little snap of us and the reindeer, which our girls thought was hilarious,” she says. “Service with a smile.”

Community spirit

News.title: Guimaraes will not force Newcastle exit like Isak, says Howe
News.content:
Newcastle will welcome Liverpool, with whom Keegan enjoyed success in the 1970s, to St James’ Park for their Premier League opener, and the two sides are in talks over a suitable pre-match tribute. Flowers, messages and mementos have been laid outside Newcastle’s ground since Keegan’s death on Monday, including a heartfelt message penned by fellow club legend Alan Shearer, which read: “I hope you realised how much you meant, to me, to this club, to everyone. Thank you does not seem enough. Rest In Peace Boss. Alan Shearer.”

With regards to the football, there is an acceptance among Newcastle supporters that, having finished 12th in the Premier League last season and lost Anthony Gordon, Kieran Trippier and Sandro Tonali, this is a summer of transition. The uncertainty surrounding the future of £100m-rated club captain Bruno Guimarães, who is on the radar of Arsenal, will be a concern; Newcastle will be keen to avoid a repeat of the furore that circled Alexander Isak’s departure last summer. Guimarães will join the team next week following his World Cup exploits with Brazil and is expected to take part in Newcastle’s La Manga training camp, which starts on July 31.

Summer signings Sean Steur and Ewen Jaouen were each handed 45 minutes in the behind-closed-doors victory over Darlington, during which Howe used different XIs for the two halves. Bazoumana Touré – the £50m winger acquired from Hoffenheim – is expected to feature today having returned from his post-World Cup holiday. Yesterday Newcastle announced the arrival of midfielder Aladji Bamba, the France youth international, from Monaco and he was immediately integrated into team training. News.title: How to choose a sports bra, with advice from a netball player, bra fitter and scientist
News.content:
How do you tell if a sports bra is the wrong size?

One of the biggest mistakes shoppers make is assuming that if a sports bra feels tight, that’s enough. In reality, support comes from the right fit rather than simply compressing your chest.

Cardwell advises thoroughly testing a sports bra by moving in it in the same way as you will during the sport you will be doing. “Your breasts don’t just move up and down,” she says. “They move all around – circles, up, down, left, right. We want to try and restrict that as much as possible, but not to the extreme where you’re not able to breathe.”

What is a high impact sports bra?

High-impact sports bras are designed for activities where your breasts experience the greatest movement, such as running, HIIT, tennis and netball. Their job is to minimise breast movement in every direction, helping reduce discomfort while allowing you to move more efficiently.

To measure how high-impact a sports bra is, Wakefield-Scurr asks women to run in a laboratory, both without a bra and while wearing different sports bras. “For a bra to be classed as high support, it has to reduce breast movement above certain thresholds,” she says. “If your breasts move 10 centimetres without a bra and five centimetres in a sports bra, that bra has reduced breast movement by 50 per cent.”

In the lab, Wakefield-Scurr and her team found that “if you run in low support compared with high support, you reduce your stride length by four centimetres. Four centimetres might not sound like a lot, but over the course of a marathon, those four centimetres add up to around a mile.” This proves that wearing a high-support bra doesn’t just keep you comfortable, but it can improve your athletic performance.

Cardwell, who wears a double G cup, says high-impact support has improved dramatically in recent years. “There has been a lot more research into high-impact sports bras, especially for larger-chested women.” She also warns against assuming that every sports bra offers the same level of support. “If it’s the same material as a smaller cup size, it’s probably not going to be sufficient for someone like me with double Gs.”

How often should you replace your sports bra?

There’s no set rule for replacing a sports bra, according to Wakefield-Scurr. This is because its lifespan depends more on how you care for it than how often you wear it. “The lifespan of a sports bra is affected more by how you wash and dry it than by how often you wear it,” she says. In one of her team’s studies, support dropped by around a third after 25 washes. “Always follow the washing instructions,” she advises. “You’d be surprised how many sports bras should be hand washed or washed at a lower temperature.”

Looking after your sports bra properly will help it last longer, but no bra lasts forever. Once the underband loses its elasticity or the support noticeably decreases, it’s time to replace it to ensure you have the right level of support.
