The manhunt is ongoing.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

World.title: Self-dressing clothes could help older adults
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Most of us get dressed every day without thinking twice about it. However, a stiff shoulder can make pulling on a shirt surprisingly difficult, while balance problems can turn a simple pair of pants into a real challenge. That is what makes a new invention from South Korea's KAIST and Stanford University worth watching.

Researchers have created self-dressing clothes with soft, air-powered robots built into the fabric. Once activated, the garment moves along the body and helps guide itself into place, even while the wearer moves. The technology remains an early research project, but it shows how future clothing could help older adults get dressed with less assistance and stay independent at home longer.

CyberGuy Live: Missed "Sick of Spam?" Get the replay and checklist

Our free CyberGuy Live class, "Sick of Spam?" , has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our spam-stopping checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you step by step through simple ways to reduce robocalls, spam texts, junk email and unwanted messages. You’ll also learn how to curb political texts, clean up your inbox and spot messages that could put your personal information at risk.

Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.

NEW YORK SCHOOL DISTRICT TO DEPLOY HUMANOID ROBOT IN CLASSROOMS THIS FALL

How self-dressing clothes could support independence

Getting dressed ranks among the basic activities that often determine whether someone can live independently. When mobility or dexterity declines, people may need a spouse, family member or professional caregiver to help with a deeply personal routine.

The researchers behind the project say dressing challenges can reduce autonomy and increase reliance on caregivers. They designed the system for people with limited mobility, including older adults and those recovering from injuries. Stanford researchers have also identified dressing assistance as an important use for future home robots. The university says assistive technology could help older adults remain in their homes as caregiving needs increase.

Why dressing can become physically difficult

Dressing requires more movement than many people realize. You need to reach behind your body, lift your arms and shift your weight while handling fabric. Arthritis may make gripping or pulling clothing painful. Meanwhile, shoulder problems can limit your reach. Recovery from hip or knee surgery can also make bending difficult.

Balance adds another concern. Pulling on pants often requires someone to stand briefly on one leg or bend toward the floor. For a person who already feels unsteady, that familiar routine can become stressful. Self-dressing clothes could eventually reduce some of that reaching and pulling. However, researchers still need clinical studies to learn how well the system works for people with real mobility limitations.

How KAIST and Stanford's robotic clothing works

The researchers call their system SWAG, which stands for Self-Wearing Adaptive Garment. Instead of placing a large robotic arm next to the person, the team built flexible robotic tubes into the clothing. Air pressure causes these soft structures to unfold and grow along the body.

The movement turns the garment inside out as it advances. That approach allows the clothing to follow the person's shape while reducing friction between the fabric and skin. Think of ivy growing around a wall or tree. The plant advances from its tip rather than dragging its entire length forward. The soft robot uses a similar motion, which helps it follow curves and move across different surfaces.

A rainy bike ride sparked the robotic clothing idea

The idea began when KAIST postdoctoral researcher Nam Gyun Kim was riding his bike when it began to rain. As he kept moving, he wondered how helpful it would be if a raincoat could put itself on.

That simple idea led to a much bigger thought. Instead of making your body do all the pulling, reaching and twisting, what if the clothing could move into place on its own? From there, Kim and the research team began developing garments that use soft robotics to help dress the person wearing them.

How fast self-dressing clothes can work

Kim says putting on a full suit takes about 10 seconds. The published paper provides additional timing from individual demonstrations. A jacket moved into place in about 13 seconds, while the pants demonstration took roughly 21 seconds. A sleeve prototype took about 14 seconds.

The researchers tested sleeves, jackets and pants. Their results showed that the garments could unfold along the body while keeping contact forces within the team's safety limits. The system also relies on its physical design instead of a complicated control program. That could eventually help simplify the hardware needed for dressing assistance.

Why soft robotic clothing could feel more natural

Many existing dressing robots use rigid mechanical arms. Those systems must handle loose fabric while carefully avoiding uncomfortable contact with the person. They may also require the person to hold a fixed pose while the robot completes the task. That setup could feel awkward inside a bedroom or bathroom.

The KAIST and Stanford design takes a different approach by placing the robotic mechanism inside the garment. The clothing becomes the helper. Because the system uses soft materials, it can bend around the body rather than approaching it with a hard mechanical structure. KAIST says this design reduces physical strain and supports safer contact.

COULD A PAINT-ON ELECTRONIC TATTOO SPOT HEART ATTACKS?

Where self-dressing clothes could be used first

Older adults and people with disabilities represent a major potential use for the technology. KAIST also sees possibilities for rehabilitation patients who need temporary assistance after an injury or medical procedure. However, industrial workplaces may adopt the idea sooner.

Semiconductor employees frequently put on protective cleanroom clothing. Emergency workers may also need to suit up quickly while carrying other equipment. The researchers believe air-powered garments could help people put on protective clothing without relying heavily on their hands. The published study also discusses possible medical uses, such as helping healthcare workers apply protective coverings or compression bandages. Those applications remain potential future directions.

What self-dressing clothes still need to prove

The current system remains a research prototype connected to a pneumatic base station. Researchers have yet to announce a consumer price or release date. Several everyday questions remain unanswered. The garments would need to fit different body shapes and movement patterns. Designers would also need to address washing, storage and portable air power.

The research team says future versions may use adjustable sheaths or elastic materials to fit a wider range of bodies. The researchers also want to automate the garment-loading process and improve the controls.

Most importantly, the team says clinical trials involving people with mobility impairments will be essential. Those tests could show whether the clothing feels comfortable and works reliably outside the lab. Researchers also need to explore how the garment comes off. The current work concentrates mainly on dressing, while automated removal remains a future possibility.

What this means to you

You probably will not find robotic clothing hanging in a local store anytime soon. Yet this research gives us a useful preview of where assistive technology may be heading. For you or someone you care about, the biggest benefit could be control over a private daily routine. Clothing that handles part of the pulling and positioning could make mornings less tiring.

It could also delay the point when someone needs another person present simply to get dressed. That possibility still depends on testing, affordability and a design people feel comfortable wearing.

Kurt's key takeaways

Self-dressing clothes may sound unusual, but the need behind them is easy to understand. Arthritis, limited mobility or recovery from surgery can make getting dressed frustrating and exhausting. For older adults, a garment that helps guide itself into place could mean more privacy, less reliance on a caregiver and more confidence starting the day. The KAIST and Stanford system still has a long way to go. Researchers need to make it portable, test it with people who have mobility challenges and prove it can work safely in a home. Even so, the idea shows how technology could support independence through something as familiar as the clothes you already wear.

"Shark Tank" star Daymond John is giving fans some blunt advice on how to be successful in business.

When speaking to Fox News Digital at Fanatics Fest, the 57-year-old businessman shared that to have a successful business, you have to build it around "something that you love."

"If you're starting something that you love, you have to want to do it for free. I always say to kids, you know, you got to get paid for what you'd do for free, you'd be able to sell whatever you would buy. So, any business is a great business. Emptying garbage is a great business if you really love it. If you're doing it just for money though, you'll be screwed. Even Kevin O'Leary, you think he does it for money? No, he just likes complicated structures that manage his downside. But at the end of the day, he likes the chess game."

The reality TV star began working at a young age, developing his entrepreneurial spirit before founding FUBU ("For Us, By Us") in 1992 along with three of his childhood friends.

DIGITAL ENTREPRENEUR CREDITS THE WORLD CUP WITH TEACHING ABOUT SOCCER AND BOOSTING HER MONTHLY INCOME

Now a global fashion brand, the business began with John sewing wool hats and T-shirts himself in his mother's house in Queens, New York.

"First of all, I was frustrated by Timberland, and a couple of other people and brands that 'didn’t make clothes for African Americans,'" he told The Source Magazine. "That was why I initially created FUBU. It was my love of fashion as well and my love for music. And I felt that no longer did we have to have the 'make it and they will come theory' like other designers."

He continued: "I was a designer who actually respected the community I was selling to, and it was fun. It was an exciting time. Hip-hop was young and fresh, and I was just happy to wear the clothes that I was making as well as seeing artists and other people wear the clothes that I was making for them."

WATCH: ‘SHARK TANK’ STAR DAYMOND JOHN SHARES WHAT WILL GET YOU ‘SCREWED’ IN BUSINESS

After turning FUBU into a global fashion brand, John joined the original cast of "Shark Tank" in 2009, alongside Barbara Corcoran, O'Leary, Robert Herjavec and Kevin Harrington.

As a shark, John has invested in a number of businesses, helping entrepreneurs get them off the ground. Some of his most famous investments include Bombas and Bubba's-Q Boneless Ribs.

"I always look for the person first — before the idea," he told Inc. about his investing philosophy. "I need to know that they are going to get the right information, and not go off and make mistakes without at least trying to educate themselves. I value an entrepreneur I can get behind and trust because I know they are attempting to move forward in life."

While at Fanatics Fest, a Comic-Con style celebration and immersive sports festival, John told Fox News Digital he was looking forward to experiencing everything the festival had to offer as a fan.

"I haven't gotten to see most of it, but for three years in, I mean, this is nuts, right? It's everything from WWE to UFC, to, of course, all the sports stuff, the signing, the trading, all of the celebrities and the sports people here. I'm just here being a fan myself," he said.

World.title: Hikers face $25,000 fine after off-leash dog barked at grizzly bear on Banff National Park trail
World.content:
Two hikers are facing charges after their off-leash dog repeatedly ran toward and barked at a grizzly bear during an encounter in Banff National Park.

The incident unfolded on the Taylor Lake trail, about nine miles south-east of Lake Louise, as Washington residents Brook and Kraig Koski backed away from Bear 142, a well-known female grizzly in the park.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK

According to reports, Kraig initially encountered the bear while jogging ahead of his wife on the trail. Brook recorded the roughly 90-second video as the bear slowly followed Kraig, who walked backward while facing it and carrying bear spray.

Meanwhile, their small dog, Lola, ran freely between the hikers and the grizzly, at times barking at the bear.

"Back off!" Kraig can be heard yelling.

"You’re too close!" Brook says from behind the camera.

The hikers also repeatedly call for Lola, but at no point in the video do they appear to leash the dog or simply pick her up — despite having ample opportunity to do so.

It’s one of the most frustrating videos you’ll ever watch.

Eventually, Bear 142 leaves the trail and disappears into the woods. The encounter fortunately ended without anyone being injured, but Parks Canada wardens were able to identify the hikers after the video was posted online and racked up millions of views.

WILDLIFE PHOTOGRAPHER STAYS ICE-COLD AS MASSIVE BROWN BEAR WALKS RIGHT UP TO HIS CAMERA

The pair now face regulatory charges under the Canada National Parks Act for having an off-leash dog in a national park. Pets are required to be secured on a leash no longer than three meters, and the hikers could face fines of up to $25,000 if convicted.

"Failure to keep your pets leashed in the national parks poses risks to pets and wildlife," Parks Canada spokesperson James Eastham said in a statement. "Bears and other wildlife may react aggressively toward dogs they view as threats, resulting in their injury or death."

Nick de Ruyter, program director of WildSmart for the Biosphere Institute of the Bow Valley, praised Parks Canada for filing charges because "there was so much time in the video to grab the dog and put it on a leash."

"The safety of them, their pets and other people is far more important than getting that video," he said.

Exactly.

As someone who hikes with my dog all the time, this is the kind of behavior that makes responsible dog owners want to pull their hair out.

Keeping a dog leashed in bear country is not an arbitrary rule designed to ruin anyone’s fun. It protects the dog, the wildlife and every other hiker who may encounter an already-agitated animal farther down the trail.

Instead, Lola was allowed to run around barking at a grizzly while her owners repeatedly yelled her name and continued filming.

This is how dogs get banned from trails. It's how responsible owners who follow the rules end up losing access.

"Off-leash dogs can also cause wildlife stress, leading to them avoiding important habitats and sources of food," Eastham said. "Always keep your pets on leash when visiting national parks."

Bear 142 is estimated to be approximately 16 years old and is the daughter of Bear 122, better known as "The Boss." She has raised several cubs in Banff National Park and lost one earlier this year after it was struck and killed by a train.

Grizzly bears are considered a threatened species in Alberta.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

In this case, the hikers were fortunate. The dog was fortunate. And Bear 142 was fortunate that an entirely avoidable encounter did not end much worse.

World.title: ROBERT MAGINNIS: The Pentagon's plan to seize Iran's uranium isn't a raid. It's an invasion
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The Pentagon has reportedly revived an extraordinary option for President Donald Trump: Send thousands of American troops deep into Iran to seize enriched uranium from damaged and buried nuclear facilities, according to a new report.

It is being described as a raid. It would be nothing of the sort.

This would be a temporary invasion of hostile territory, launched without real surprise, against an enemy that has spent months expecting us, at sites whose defenses and contents remain uncertain. American troops might seize the objective only to become trapped in a mission with no reliable timetable and no clean exit.

TRUMP SEEKS $672M TO STOP IRANIAN NUKES AS NEGOTIATORS WEIGH FATE OF URANIUM STOCKPILE

A modern Desert One

The historical parallel is Operation Eagle Claw, the failed 1980 attempt to rescue American hostages in Tehran. President Jimmy Carter had exhausted diplomacy and sanctions after a hostage crisis that had humiliated the United States for six months, as mounting political pressure pushed him toward a complex rescue operation.

It ended at Desert One, where mechanical failures and a collision between a helicopter and a transport aircraft killed eight American servicemen before the rescue force ever reached Tehran.

US MILITARY IS POWERFUL ENOUGH TO CRUSH ENEMIES, BUT CAN IT DEFEAT THEIR 'FINAL 10%?'

Today's military is far more capable, with mature special operations commands and decades of combat experience. But technology does not repeal geography, logistics or enemy action, and a president's need for a decisive result does not make a fragile plan sound.

Trump has shown the Carter analogy concerns him. When asked in June about a uranium-seizure mission, he said he considered it early and rejected it. "I didn't want to be Jimmy Carter," he said.

Harder than 1980

The reported mission would dwarf Eagle Claw in complexity. Carter's force knew roughly where the hostages were. In Iran today, we may not know precisely where the enriched uranium sits, whether it has been divided among sites, or whether Iran has already moved it. Some officials believe international inspectors have not verified its location in nearly nine months.

The Pentagon plan reportedly contemplates securing Iran's Fordow and Isfahan facilities, along with the deeply buried Pickaxe Mountain complex near Natanz, where Iran is believed to have moved centrifuges.

IRAN NUCLEAR DEAL HINGES ON IAEA ACCESS TO LONG-BLOCKED ATOMIC WEAPON SITES, EXPERTS SAY

Thousands of troops could be required, including Army Rangers, special operations forces and combat engineers. One version reportedly calls for flying in excavation equipment and building a runway to fly out roughly 450 kilograms of highly enriched uranium, some enriched to 60 percent.

Pickaxe Mountain alone shows the scale of the problem. Analysts believe it sits more than 300 feet underground, deeper than the Fordow plant the U.S. struck last year. Open-source evidence does not place uranium there at all; the mountain may hold centrifuges instead, and American forces could fight their way inside only to discover the objective had already disappeared.

No element of surprise

Iran knows the likely targets and has spent months preparing entrances, roads and defenses. At Isfahan, tunnel entrances believed to hold much of Iran's enriched uranium reportedly remain backfilled with dirt, reinforced with mines and roadblocks to complicate any ground approach. As one former National Security Council official noted, the sites are fixed and both sides know which facilities American forces would likely approach.

American aircraft might suppress Iran's air defenses and deliver an assault force. That is only the first step. Troops would then have to control roads, tunnel portals and an airfield for heavy cargo aircraft, while engineers bring in heavy equipment and other troops secure a wide perimeter. Inside, they could confront collapsed concrete, mines, poor ventilation and armed defenders in confined passages. Every hour favors Iran.

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps would likely respond on multiple fronts: striking American bases, disrupting shipping through Hormuz and activating proxies in Iraq, Syria and Yemen. Tehran would not need to defeat American forces outright, only deny them the objective by collapsing tunnels, contaminating the site or trapping personnel inside.

The longer our forces remain, the more dangerous the mission becomes. What began as a raid becomes a defended American lodgment hundreds of miles inside Iran. The moment American engineers begin building an airstrip on Iranian soil, the raid becomes an invasion.

Why not seal it instead?

That raises the question Washington should ask before sending a single soldier underground: Why not deny access to the facilities rather than occupy them?

If the uranium is trapped inside damaged tunnels, the wiser course may be to collapse every known entrance and access route, then maintain surveillance and strike any effort to reopen the site. Iran might carve a concealed entrance or move the material first — but seal, monitor and re-strike may be far more sustainable than sending thousands of Americans into an underground maze.

The goal should be making reopening slow, visible, costly and vulnerable to another strike, not pretending the mountain can never reopen.

Washington should keep demanding International Atomic Energy Agency access and verified accounting of the material as the price of any further relief, paired with sanctions, interdiction and verified international custody of the stockpile.

The Carter trap

Trump is not Carter, and this is not 1980. But both presidents confronted an adversary that refused to yield and mounting pressure to deliver one dramatic operation that could break the stalemate. I will not call Trump desperate; that claims knowledge of his state of mind outsiders lack. But the administration plainly faces pressure to convert tactical success into a visible strategic victory, and seizing Iran's uranium for display in American custody would offer precisely that image. Wars punish leaders who confuse a powerful image with a durable outcome.

Wars are not won by counting targets destroyed, but by producing a durable political outcome. American forces have punished Iran and badly damaged its military, but an open-ended ground commitment could still turn success into failure.

Before proceeding, the administration owes the country answers: Do we know where the uranium is? Can we reach it? How many troops are needed to hold the perimeter? What happens when Iran counterattacks? And before placing thousands of Americans on Iranian soil, has Washington secured the legal authority and public support for a ground war?

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Most importantly, how do we get our troops home?

Desert One failed before the rescue force reached Tehran. A uranium-seizure mission could reach the mountain, breach the tunnels and still fail because getting in is not the same as getting out. The real test is not whether America can reach the objective. It is whether the objective justifies the cost when a less dangerous strategy may achieve the same strategic result.

World.title: Missing Grand Canyon hiker, 83, rescued after getting separated from companion
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

An 83-year-old hiker who vanished in a remote stretch of Grand Canyon National Park after separating from his companion was found alive after an intense all-night search across rugged burn-scarred terrain, officials said Thursday.

Gerald Guinn, an experienced outdoorsman from Kanab, Utah, was found around 6:30 p.m. on Tuesday during a National Park Service helicopter search, about 2.5 miles from where he was last seen on the park's North Rim, according to the National Park Service and the Kane County Sheriff's Office.

Guinn disappeared Monday after he and his hiking companion intentionally split up while taking a short hike around 12:30 p.m. in search of a nearby historic object in a remote area near the park's northeastern boundary, the sheriff’s office said. While his hiking partner found the object, Guinn never showed up. After several hours of searching, the other hiker called for help.

SEARCH UNDERWAY FOR AUSTRALIAN WOMAN WHO VANISHED AFTER SENDING MESSAGE ABOUT GOING FOR A HIKE NEAR LAS VEGAS

Search crews from Grand Canyon National Park, Coconino County Search and Rescue , and Kane County Search and Rescue spent the night looking for Guinn. Teams searched on foot through burned forest, the sheriff’s office said, while drones, search dogs and helicopters helped cover the remote area.

On Tuesday, investigators were able to narrow the search after receiving a cellphone ping from Guinn's phone. When a National Park Service helicopter later spotted him, Guinn waved to the crew overhead, the sheriff's office said.

The helicopter couldn't land because of the steep, rugged terrain, so a Kane County Search and Rescue team hiked about 1.5 miles to reach him. Deputies said Guinn was in good spirits but was cold and unable to walk. Rescuers gave him water and warm clothing while deciding how to get him out safely.

FIREFIGHTERS, POLICE PULL YOUNG WOMAN FROM SEWAGE-FILLED RAVINE AFTER DAYS TRAPPED IN 104-DEGREE HEAT

With darkness setting in, a helicopter rescue was no longer an option. Instead, a paramedic was flown to the scene, and about 20 rescuers took turns carrying Guinn through the rough terrain in a rescue stretcher, clearing fallen trees and marking hazards along the way until they reached a nearby road around 1:30 a.m. — a day and a half after Guinn first set out on the hike.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Guinn was checked by emergency medical personnel and released, according to the sheriff's office.

The National Park Service thanked Coconino County Search and Rescue and Kane County Search and Rescue for helping bring the search to a successful end.

World.title: Manhunt underway for suspect with ‘Islamist’ ties after deadly Berlin Pride attack
World.content:
A manhunt is underway for a 21-year-old suspect after a vehicle was driven into a crowd near Berlin’s Pride festival on Saturday night, killing a woman and injuring 29 others.

Subscribe to read this story ad-free Get unlimited access to ad-free articles and exclusive content.

The suspect is also believed to have attacked people with a bladed object, authorities said. The attack happened in Tiergarten park around 10 p.m. local time, near the Brandenburg Gate landmark in the German capital.

Three of the injured people have life-threatening injuries, Berlin’s fire department spokesman Dominik Pretz said Sunday morning, adding that eight are seriously injured.

Police released a photo of a suspect, named as 21-year-old Abdul B., who officials said is known to be a “radicalized” member of “Islamist circles” in Berlin.

Police and prosecutors asked for help in finding a 21-year-old, whom they identified as Abdul B. Handout / Berlin Police

“Everything we are seeing here indicates that we have experienced an Islamist attack,” German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told a press conference on Sunday.

He said that the suspect is a German citizen of Lebanese background known to police after committing crimes in the past. Abdul B. had previously been sentenced to one year and 10 months in prison in Berlin, he said, which was commuted to parole. He did not say what the sentence was for.

“We cannot rule out the possibility that further terrorist attacks might take place,” he said, adding that Germany’s threat level would be raised following the attack.

The attack was outside the secure festival area, Dobrindt said, adding that many of those attacked were going to or from the festival site.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has condemned the incident in Berlin as “a heinous act.”

“They wanted us to treat each other with kindness and tolerance. This is an attack on our society,” he wrote on X, adding that the attack will be investigated with the “utmost severity.”

Saturday “should have been a day of joy, visibility and freedom,” Alfonso Pantisano, the Berlin state government’s queer liaison officer, wrote on social media.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen expressed her sympathy to the victims on Sunday, saying the Pride event stands for “freedom, dignity, and equality.”

“Every person should be able to live, love, and stand up for their rights without fear,” she wrote on social media.

Police officers inspect the car that allegedly was driven into people, killing one person and injuring dozens more before crashing on a tree in the Tiergarten park on the outskirts of the Christopher Street Day parade in Berlin. John Macdougall / AFP via Getty Images

A white vehicle suspected of being used in the attack has also been pictured inside the police cordon. The vehicle appears to have crashed into a tree.

The suspect is described as having a slim build, around 1.9 meters (6-foot-3) tall with black hair, a black hoodie and white pants.

Sunday’s notice warned the public to avoid “direct contact” with the suspect, saying that he may be armed and dangerous.

Hundreds of thousands of people had come to Berlin for one of Europe’s largest LGBTQ+ celebrations on Saturday. The parade had passed through the park earlier in the day.

Pride events were called off around 10:15 p.m., shortly after the attack, with all further celebrations canceled in the aftermath.

World.title: Influencer killed by husband after she accused him of pedophilia on TikTok
World.content:
A social media influencer was killed by her estranged husband less than two weeks after she posted on TikTok accusing him of pedophilia, according to police and court records.

Subscribe to read this story ad-free Get unlimited access to ad-free articles and exclusive content.

Sara Gilson was fatally shot Thursday in Owasso, Oklahoma, by husband Jeremiah Duffey, who went by Shawn Duffey on social media, according to the Owasso Police Department. She was 43.

A little over a month earlier, on June 10, she filed and was granted an emergency protective order against Duffey after police informed her he’d been accused the day prior of molesting a minor.

On July 11, Gilson posted a video on TikTok, where she had more than 30,000 followers, accusing Duffey of pedophilia.

“Preparing for when Netflix drops a documentary about my soon to be ex husband who I just found out is a pedophile,” Gilson wrote.

The video referenced a popular social media trend that mimics Netflix documentaries, with users pretending to sit for a tell-all interview. Her caption read: “I wish I was joking. #plottwist #netflix #documentary.”

Less than two weeks later, Gilson was killed.

On June 9, about a month before Gilson posted the video, a girl and a parent told police that Duffey, who coached the girl’s traveling basketball team, inappropriately touched her during an event at an elementary school earlier that evening, police said. Another team coach saw what happened and immediately intervened and reported it to the girl’s parent, police said.

“Similar conduct by this coach towards this particular juvenile player was reported to have occurred over an extended period of time, in multiple law enforcement jurisdictions, across multiple states prior to this incident,” police said Saturday.

Duffey fled and had not been seen by police since.

Because Duffey was a member of the Osage tribe and the incident at the school happened on tribal land, police said, they submitted the case for a charge of lewd molestation of a minor to the U.S. attorney’s office for review, “ending the jurisdiction of the Owasso Police Department over this reported incident.”

Following the report, police contacted Gilson and gave her information on how to seek an emergency protective order.

She did just that and the order was granted June 10, Tulsa County court records show. Duffey was ordered to stay 100 yards away from Gilson and her home at all times. The attorney who represented Duffey did not immediately respond to a request for comment Saturday.

On Thursday, officers responded to a domestic violence incident at a residence in the city of Collinsville at 11:16 p.m. after a 911 call in which dispatchers heard a woman screaming followed by “what sounded to be a gunshot,” police said. Dispatchers attempted to call back but got no answer.

Moments later, a boy called 911 from a neighbor’s home and said his stepfather had shot his mother, police said. When officers arrived at the home, they found Gilson and Duffey dead from apparent gunshot wounds to the head, police said.

Police are still investigating, but they said the deaths appear to be a murder-suicide.

Gilson’s son was taken into protective custody and later released to a parent who wasn’t involved in the incident, authorities said. Gilson leaves behind the son and a daughter.

“Sara was an incredible mom. Her children were the center of her world, and everything she did was for them,” an online fundraiser set up for the kids said. “She loved them fiercely, worked hard to provide for them, and dreamed of giving them the best life possible.”

If you or someone you know is in crisis, call or text 988 or go to 988lifeline.org to reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, or visit SpeakingOfSuicide.com/resources.

World.title: Ryan Coogler announces David Jonsson as the new Black Panther
World.content:
There’s a new Black Panther, and his name is David Jonsson.

Subscribe to read this story ad-free Get unlimited access to ad-free articles and exclusive content.

Director Ryan Coogler announced at Marvel’s San Diego Comic-Con panel on Saturday that Jonsson would be assuming the role.

Jonsson will play T’Challa’s son in “Black Panther 3,” which will be out on Dec. 15, 2028. Coogler is returning to direct the third movie in the series.

David Jonsson and Ryan Coogler onstage during the Marvel Studios panel on Saturday. Joe Scarnici / Getty Images for Disney

“Thank you to this amazing family that I have the honor and the privilege and the blessing to join,” Jonsson said onstage after Coogler shared the news. “I actually don’t want to say too much because I want to let this screen do the talking.”

The crowd roared with applause upon learning the news.

In the first Black Panther film, T’Challa was played by Chadwick Boseman, who died of colon cancer in 2020 after the movie premiered and while Coogler was working on the film’s sequel.

His role was somewhat assumed in “Black Panther: Wakanda Forever” by Letitia Wright, who played T’Challa’s sister, Shuri.

The news of Jonsson’s casting appears to be the true passing of the torch, though.

His role, Prince T’Challa II, was introduced in the second Black Panther installment, but the third film will see him coming of age and taking over.

Jonsson is most known for his roles in Stephen King’s “The Long Walk,” “Alien: Romulus” and as Gus Sackey in the first two seasons of “Industry.”

In other major casting news, Ryan Gosling was revealed to be the star of the upcoming Ghost Rider film set to hit theaters in 2028. That film will be helmed by “Deadpool & Wolverine” director Shawn Levy.

Ironically Gosling’s long time partner, actress Eva Mendes, co-starred as the love interest in the 2007 “Ghost Rider” film opposite Nicholas Cage.

World.title: U.S. forgoes strikes on Iran, but conflict escalates in the Red Sea
World.content:
The Iran war ​broadened over the weekend despite a pause in U.S. strikes, as Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis attacked Saudi oil installations along the Red Sea coast and Iran ‌accused Ukraine of targeting one of its vessels in the Caspian Sea.

Subscribe to read this story ad-free Get unlimited access to ad-free articles and exclusive content.

The U.S. military said Saturday that its naval blockade against Iran “remains in full effect” but did not explain why it halted a streak of 13 nights of escalating strikes.

There were also no weekend reports of attacks by Iran on neighbors, similar to its daily rejoinders to the U.S. attacks.

U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” that a pause in strikes was due to ongoing talks between the two countries.

“What the president is doing right now, as we’ve seen all along, is giving some talks some space,” he said. “Talks are ongoing.”

Waltz added that while talks were ongoing at the highest levels of the Iranian and U.S. governments, there was “internal fighting” on the Iranian side.

“Some are seeking the guidance of the supreme leader,” he said. “Others want to move into a different direction, and that makes it hugely challenging.”

Iran ​will halt its own attacks as long as the United ⁠States maintains its pause on strikes, but Tehran remains skeptical of U.S. ⁠intentions, a ​senior Iranian source told Reuters on Sunday.

“Iran’s ⁠position remains ‘attack for attack’: ​if ⁠the attacks stop, ‌Iran will also halt its operations. That message ‌has already been conveyed ‌to the United States,” the source told Reuters, ⁠a day after Washington halted attacks following 13 successive nights of airstrikes.

“There is more skepticism than optimism about ‌the halt in attacks. ​The prevailing view ‌is that ⁠the pause is ⁠tactical rather than genuine,” the ‌source added.

Trump has decided, for now, to back away from plans to ramp up attacks on Iran, ⁠The New York Times reported Saturday, citing two people briefed on the discussion.

The president and his advisers, the newspaper said, have concerns about expanding the conflict, depleting ​defense stockpiles, alienating Middle East Gulf allies and affecting energy supplies and the global economy.

Vice President JD Vance and Gen. Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, ​both raised concerns about the U.S. munitions stockpile with Trump during a White House meeting on Friday, a U.S. official told CNN.

Operations are “on a hold,” a Department of Defense source told the broadcaster on Saturday.

Despite the Gulf lull, Saturday’s fighting between Iran’s Houthi allies and Saudi Arabia showed that the war, which has already disrupted energy supplies through the Strait of Hormuz, could affect a second major ​shipping route and reignite Yemen’s civil war.

Separately, Iran’s Foreign Ministry accused Ukraine of attacking an Iranian commercial vessel in the Caspian Sea, saying one sailor was killed and another injured.

The ​ministry summoned Ukraine’s chargé d’affaires in Tehran to protest over an attack it described as “hostile and criminal,” state news agency IRNA said.

The Iranian denunciation coincided with comments by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy that Kyiv had ‌noted Russia ⁠was passing on to Iran its satellite observations in the Middle East to enable it to direct strikes in the region.

Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group struck sites belonging to Saudi state oil company Aramco in the cities of Jizan and Yanbu on Saturday.

A large column of smoke rose from the direction of the Aramco refinery in Jizan, near the Yemeni border, video on social media verified by Reuters showed. The refinery can process up to 400,000 barrels of crude oil ​daily.

Two Asia-based trading sources said they had been ​informed of potential damage to fuel ⁠and oil storage sites at Jizan. Aramco did not respond to requests for comment.

In Yanbu, two missiles aimed at oil installations were intercepted. Yanbu, Saudi Arabia’s main Red Sea oil port, has become a key route for Saudi oil skirting the Strait of Hormuz, ​which Iran has blockaded.

In Yemen, officials said the air force of the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized government, which has ​opposed the Houthis for ⁠more than a decade, struck Houthi sites in the Marib and al-Jawf provinces.

The officials said both sides in Yemen’s civil war were mobilizing forces along the front.

Saudi Arabia has led an Arab coalition battling the Houthis since the Iran-aligned fighters captured Yemen’s capital, Sanaa.

The civil war, in which famine and fighting killed hundreds of thousands, has been paused by a ceasefire since ⁠2022.

But that ​truce broke down this month, with the Houthis effectively joining the wider war their Iranian allies have ​waged since being attacked by the United States and Israel five months ago.

The Houthis have declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia over the past week, and Houthi leader Abdul Malik al-Houthi said all Saudi oil ​facilities could be targets.

World.content: Former FDA head praises response to cyclospora outbreak, but says it's not "under control yet" Former FDA commissioner Scott Gottlieb told "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" that while the current administration has done a good job isolating and identifying the cyclospora pathogen, the spread isn't "under control yet" and that federal officials need to do more to communicate with the American public. Gottlieb also discussed skyrocketing measles cases and whether that trend is likely to continue.

World.content: Sen. John Kennedy says U.S. should "stay the course" in Iran Senator John Kennedy said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" that he supports President Trump's goals in Iran and believes the U.S. should "stay the course" in the region, but said officials should share more information about the conflict with the American public. He also explained why he doesn't yet support the U.S.' civil nuclear power deal with Saudi Arabia, and he called for the passage of the SAVE America Act, the contentious elections-related bill championed by Mr. Trump.

World.title: Home, not alone: Helping aging seniors in rural America
World.content:
In North Dakota, small farming towns like Hebron and Glen Ullin, where there are many retirees, have withstood all manner of challenges. Despite the difficulties, 98-year-old Mae Buchli, whom we met back in 2025, is determined to live out her days out here. "We decided we're not going to move, 'cause we want to stay home," she told us. "You know how that is."

Across the country, rural America is growing older faster than urban America. According to the USDA, the number of counties where at least 20% of residents are over the age of 65 has nearly tripled since 2010.

And it's in those older populations where the health risks associated with loneliness and social isolation are more common.

Eighty-eight-year-old Lynda Hoerauf knows no other life – nor does she want another one. "It's so opposite, these little rural towns, from cities and things," she said. But she wouldn't have it any other way. "No, I wouldn't. I absolutely wouldn't," she said.

For Hoerauf, Sundays are the worst, "because there's nothing going on."

For Father Gary Benz, who grew up on a farm nearby, this is well-worn territory. If his parishioners can't come to him, he goes to them, like 96-year-old Viola Weinhart.

Father Gary Benz visits 96-year-old parishioner Viola Weinhart. CBS News

Asked how visitations have changed his personal ministry, Father Benz replied, "It's helped me, because I think it's made me more compassionate, because my parents were in their situation. And so, I know firsthand how lonely life can be."

Weinhart says he is good company: "He spends a little time with me each week, and fills me in on the latest news, especially on the church."

In rural counties, one in five adults is age 65 or older. Even if some wanted to move to urban areas with more resources, the cost disparity would make it difficult at best.

The Rural Health Transformation Program, part of President Trump's "Big Beautiful Bill," is pouring $50 billion into providing better access for seniors to doctors and other caregivers, but there are still cracks that seniors can fall through, and they aren't always about medicine.

"Sometimes older adults, especially in the challenging years, get overlooked, forgotten," said Jane Strommen, a gerontology specialist at North Dakota State University Extension in Fargo. She's been taking more of a grass roots approach to helping rural seniors.

"People are good, and they want to help their fellow neighbor and community member," Strommen said. "Sometimes that just takes a little bit of organizing."

Acting as our brother's or sister's keeper may sound pretty naïve, but not to the Margaret A. Cargill Philanthropies, which funded a local pilot program, directed by Strommen, called Aging in Community. "We're trying to keep it practical, and keep it simple, and something that's workable in our rural communities," Strommen said.

It essentially takes what is already there – neighbors – and encourages them to form a kind of neighborhood watch for seniors.

Kyla Sanders, a retired nurse who grew up in rural Montana, has been on board since the beginning. She's one of four regional coordinators for Aging in Community.

As part of the Aging in Community program, retired nurse Kyla Sanders visits with the elderly in isolated rural North Dakota. CBS News

On this day, we watched her bring Mae Buchli a calendar that she can hear, not see. "Oh, is that ever neat!" Buchli said.

Just a little assistance that mattered more than you might know. Sanders said, "They want to be able to be around other humans and interact and have that sense of belonging and that sense of value."

Sanders spends hours taking the roads less traveled out here, helping with everything from stopped wristwatches to filing tax returns. And she's organized game days.

She's been working for Aging in Community for five years now, and in that time, the NDSU Extension program has been able to do what no federal health care plan can necessarily provide. "Our clients are saying that they have a higher quality of life, that they feel more confident living at home, that they feel more connected to resources locally," Sanders said. "Those are three really big things for us."

So big, the program is expanding to serve 12 North Dakota counties, some of them so rural they're classified as "frontier," meaning there are six or fewer people per square mile.

Back at Lynda Hoerauf's house, our visit extended long after Kyla Sanders left, pleasantly so.

Where we talked might have mattered more than what we talked about. After all, as Hoerauf (and so many others) told us, "There's no place like home."



For more info:



Story produced by Michelle Kessel. Editor: Remington Korper.
