Unfortunately, reality is far more boring than that, and it cannot match the Argentine genius for theatrics – and I mean this as a compliment.

Spain dominated the game, with a 68% possession rate. If you can't touch the ball, you can't win. Spain took 20 shots, 11 of them on target, doubled Argentina's passes, and had a higher accuracy rate too. Argentina had Fernández sent off, while Spain kept their squad practically intact. Scaloni's substitutions didn't really make a difference, while bringing on Ferran led to a goal for Spain. Messi looked as though he had disappeared from the pitch, because he did.

So, where is all of this coming from? That's the question we put to our guests this week on Euronews. Some suggested Argentina is a country of high emotions: it's all or nothing. Football remains an area where they have dominated for decades, even as the country's economic decline became entrenched. It's a tough world; so you have to play rough and strike first.

My colleague Michael Reid, who can be forgiven for being English in this feuilleton, told Europe Today that football is far more important in Latin America than it is in Europe when it comes to the social and political fabric of the continent. The cost of losing, and what you're willing to sacrifice in order to win, is significantly higher for better or worse.

Then there's the Italian legacy, which in a country like Argentina matters.

Reid told us that, much like in the 1960s and early 1970s, when the Italians turned catenaccio into a winning strategy, Argentines have also embraced a more aggressive style of play. He also suggested that the question of why Argentina plays like that might ultimately be better answered by a psychoanalyst - which is convenient, because the country has one of the highest ratios of psychoanalysts per capita in the world. The psyche matters in sport.

And I have to give them some credit. No other country brings the theatrics, the excess, the comedy and the tragedy like Argentines do. When you look at the Malvinas issue, one could argue that it comes down to freedom of expression. For the English, there is no debate, but for Argentines, it's a legitimate political protest and is shared by many. By the way, no one knows what the Falkland Islands are in the Spanish-speaking world; everyone calls them Islas Malvinas. That's a linguistic reality, not necessarily a political statement on its own.

Nonetheless, FIFA is investigating whether Argentina breached football rules during its semi-final against England as a result, and is also studying possible penalties following a physical altercation involving Paredes after the Spain final.

Expect little from FIFA. The federation is too busy laughing all the way to the bank after a successful tournament in terms of revenue and television ratings. For the football giant, this World Cup had a clear goal: breaking into the profitable North American market. Judging by the numbers for the final broadcast simultaneously on Fox, in English, and Telemundo, in Spanish, it did.

Speaking of Infantino, this week the New York Post reported that Trump is eyeing him to lead the United Nations, replacing António Guterres, who is very much disliked by the Americans. The paper reported that the US President sees Infantino as capable of bringing the world together, unlike the "lame" candidates who have thrown their hats in the ring so far. That sounds a lot like Trump.

Lastly FIFA, if you read this, please next time kill the halftime show. We don't want BTS and Bieber; we want to watch the game with fewer breaks. The Argentines are far more entertaining than any pop star - on and off the pitch.

As always, if you have any comments, email me at maria.tadeo@euronews.com.

- Maria Tadeo

Tariffs, fines and bad blood. Who will blink first?

​Tariffs are back – sort of. This week, the US administration announced a new global tariff of 10 to 12.5%, under Section 301 of the US Trade Act. To justify the new duties, Washington argued that more than 60 countries had failed to prevent forced labour in their supply chains, and should be punished for it.

The White House says it's about protecting workers. How magnanimous, Ave Trump. Trade experts argue it's a convenient way to keep tariffs alive after the previous measures were struck down by the courts multiple times.

In case you missed it, the big "Liberation Day" tariffs were blocked by the US Supreme Court, which ruled that President Trump had exceeded his executive authority by design, earlier this year, and the temporary tariffs that replaced them were about to lapse anyway. Timing-wise, it all lines up.

Meanwhile, the EU announced it would fine Google's search business, a move that could trigger fresh tensions with Washington, as the Trump administration has long viewed Brussels' scrutiny of US tech giants as a political Trojan horse.

I sat down with our political correspondent, Luca Bertuzzi, to debrief it all.

Maria: OK, Luca - new tariffs. What does it mean for the EU?

Luca: Well, the legal basis for the new tariffs is preposterous as far as Europe is concerned. As Kaja Kallas argued, labour laws and working conditions in the EU can hardly be compared to those in the US. Leaving that aside, the irony is that these new tariffs are actually good news for the Europeans compared to others.

Maria: So, no panic in Brussels?

Luca: Not yet, but that could change. The new duties remain below the 15% ceiling of the Turnberry agreement and all exemptions are broadly respected. The focus now is on the digital regulation and how Americans may react in retaliation to the Commission fining Google this week. That's the real issue.

Maria: Indeed, but first, remind us what the Turnberry agreement is?

Luca: Last summer, the head of the Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, flew to the President's golf resort in Turnberry, Scotland, hence the name. The EU accepted tariffs that tripled from around 5% to 15% and gave it a thumbs up in a picture that still haunts the Berlaymont. The terms of the deal are clearly beneficial for the US. That was a political choice as European leaders preferred to settle rather than escalate a trade war the way China did, for example.

Maria: It wasn't really a negotiation, yet Brussels defends it...

Luca: The Europeans took some comfort in securing what Brussels called a non-stackable tariff rate – which basically means 15% is a ceiling, and the US cannot tally up other duties on top. It's cold comfort, but for companies it really matters. Brussels also locked some exemptions, but not on everything it wanted, and tariffs on steel and aluminium remain at 50% – which is prohibitive.

Maria: Who is paying these tariffs anyway?

Luca: According to the Commission's data, American importers are now paying roughly €31 billion in additional duties one year after Turnberry. That compares to €8 billion before the tariffs kicked in. It's quite a significant jump and the correlation is clear. Some of it, companies can absorb, and Trump made it clear he wanted them to, and even suggested retaliation if companies dared show the extra costs linked to tariffs on receipts. But the consumer inevitably pays too.

Maria: Tell me about Brussels hitting Google with a fresh fine this week. Why?

Luca: This fine has been a long time coming. This is about Google self-preferencing in search results and locking app developers into its ecosystem. For years, businesses have complained about what they see as unfair commercial practices – in Europe, but also in the US. So this is really not just about targeting American companies, but of course you could argue it's always easier to regulate foreign companies than your own.

Maria: It's punchy, but the amount doesn't seem much. Was it watered down?

Luca: That's true. €890 million is a small fine compared to traditional antitrust cases, usually in the order of billions of euros. But however hefty it looks on paper, it's still just a speeding ticket for a company whose revenues dwarf most national budgets. The real point is whether the Commission can actually make Google change its behaviour on commercial practices very close to its core interests. That's the real test. Not the size of the fine.

Maria: How will the US respond?

Luca: In a way, it already has. And it's not looking good. President Trump has vowed to make the EU pay a heavy price for what he sees as an attack on American companies. On Friday, he announced a trade investigation into what he called theft from the Europeans and teased a substantial retaliatory tariff. He didn't put a number on it, but you see where things are heading...

Maria: That's a real problem, because regulation is a sovereign matter, right?

Luca: The EU sees this as a red line, applying the law of the land is a matter for Europeans to decide, not foreign powers. It could set a very dangerous precedent and ultimately weaken the EU's ability to regulate the single market, its biggest economic asset.

If Brussels pulls back, it would also send a signal to other countries that it can be blackmailed into changing regulatory standards- and that opens a whole set of problems. Don't forget the Chinese are also looking at this.

Maria: Speaking of China, this week the EU also opened investigations into Chinese social media app TikTok, as well as AliExpress. What is this about?

Luca: These investigations are the result of a broader EU effort to make digital services safer, whether from illegal goods or harmful algorithms.

In this geopolitical context, it of course helps to go after Chinese companies alongside American ones – so Brussels can make the case that its rules apply to everyone, regardless of country of origin. But there is a real problem with some of these Chinese sellers and the way they track products that are banned in Europe beyond the geopolitics. Remember the Shein sex doll scandal?

Maria: The sex dolls that looked like children? That was shocking.

Luca: Correct – these are illegal goods, and there is an expectation from European consumers that regulators will do their job. And they are so easy to buy in online marketplaces. The sale of weapons is also a real issue. So these investigations do signal very serious problems beyond the politics of it all.

Thank you Luca.

BEFORE YOU GO, GET IN TOUCH

Next week, as Europe and, certainly, Brussels, prepare to wind down for the summer, I want to use this as an opportunity to give you the floor. Each weekend, I receive your feedback, suggestions and comments. Next week, I'll be answering your questions in Q&A format in this newsletter. From trade relations to enlargement, the war in Ukraine, Europe's defence plans and budget talks - get in touch this week with your questions at maria.tadeo@euronews.com.

Thank you for reading Off The Record. I'll be back next Saturday with more — make sure to subscribe here so you never miss the next issue.

Editor-in-Chief, EU News

World.title: Ukraine strikes Russian Iran-bound cargo as Iran war widens
World.content:
The battlefield in the war involving Iran is expanding, and with its entry into the dispute via long-range strikes on targets that Kyiv says are linked to the transfer of Russian military equipment to Iran, Ukraine has become one of the new players in this crisis.

 

At the same time, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the Ukrainian president, has claimed that Russia, by providing satellite information to Iran, has helped Tehran target US military facilities in the Middle East.

These developments have added new dimensions to the crisis between Iran and the United States and have tied the confrontation between Tehran and Washington to the war between Russia and Ukraine, putting Moscow's role in supporting Iran back in the spotlight.

In a post on X, the Ukrainian president said that since the beginning of July, Russian satellites have been actively monitoring the Gulf states and US military facilities in the region, and have been handing the images obtained over to Iran.

According to him, there is a "clear correlation" between Russian satellite imagery of these sites and Iranian attacks: both images taken before the attacks during Iran's preparations, and those captured afterwards to assess the damage.

Zelenskyy also claimed that on 19 and 20 July, four air bases, including two in Bahrain, one in Jordan and one in Kuwait, were within the observation range of Russian satellites.

He added that this reality must not be ignored: "Forces of evil are always seeking to make the situation worse and to widen the scope of the crisis."

He went on to say that Russia must be stopped, this war must end, and pressure on the "aggressor state" has to be effective.

Ukraine announced on Saturday that in its long-range attacks it had targeted vessels in the Caspian Sea which, according to Kyiv, were being used to transport military cargo between Iran and Russia.

Iran says that one of the targeted vessels was an Iranian commercial ship and that one sailor was killed and several others were injured in the attack.

On Saturday, in response to Ukraine's strike, Tehran summoned the country's acting chargé d'affaires in Tehran to the foreign ministry to lodge an official protest over the attack.

In this photo, published on the official website of Iran's army on Monday 27 November 2023, the destroyer AP Photo

IRNA reported that during this meeting Iran stressed that "the Islamic Republic will firmly defend its security and national interests and will not leave attacks on the lives and property of its citizens unanswered".

Meanwhile, as Iran's foreign ministry reiterated Tehran's right to respond, some Iranian social media users have been calling for retaliation using the country's Kheibar Shekan ballistic missiles.

In unofficial comments posted online, several users criticised what they described as the Foreign Ministry's "weak diplomacy." One widely shared comment read: "As long as this weak diplomacy remains in government, every fox will see itself as a lion against us."

Other users highlighted the range and capabilities of Iran's missile arsenal, arguing that Tehran should demonstrate its deterrence.

In the same context, former Iranian lawmaker Nezameddin Mousavi reacted to what he described as a Ukrainian military attack on an Iranian commercial vessel in the Caspian Sea.

Mousavi said: "The response to this fireworks display in the Caspian Sea should be delivered in the Black Sea." He added that Ukraine's alleged action should prompt Iran to reconsider its self-imposed 2,000-kilometre limit on the range of its ballistic missiles.

However, Ukraine has presented a different account of the incident. Ukraine’s Ambassador to Israel, Yevgen Korniychuk, claimed that the vessel targeted by Ukraine in the Caspian Sea on Saturday was carrying components for drones and missiles that were being transported to Iran.

Speaking in an interview with Israel’s N12 on Sunday, Korniychuk rejected Iran’s claim that the ship was carrying civilian cargo, saying Ukraine considers such shipments to be legitimate military targets.

He added that this was not the first time Ukraine had targeted what he described as military supplies linked to Iran, and said Kyiv expects similar operations to continue in the future.

“Israel and Ukraine are fighting the same enemy,” Korniychuk said, describing the two countries as being on “different sides of the same evil axis.”

At the same time, Iran's foreign ministry said that Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi condemned the attack in a phone call with EU Foreign Chief Kaja Kallas, and called for a response from the UN Security Council, the European Union and the international community.

The call between Araghchi and Kallas took place only two days after the European Union imposed a new round of sanctions on Iran for human rights violations.

On 24 July, Kaja Kallas announced on X that the European Union had introduced new restrictive measures against Iranian judges responsible for "serious human rights violations", including the persecution of political opponents and religious minorities.

Trump: Russia and China will not give weapons to Iran

Zelenskyy's comments came a day after US President Donald Trump said that Russia and China would not supply arms to Iran.

In a post on the social network Truth Social, Trump wrote that Chinese President Xi Jinping had told him during their recent meeting in Beijing that China "under no circumstances" would give or sell weapons to the Islamic Republic of Iran; this also applies to Chinese companies.

Truth Social RealDonaltrump Truth Social RealDonaltrump

Trump also said that Russian President Vladimir Putin had assured him that Moscow too would not sell weapons to Iran.

"Therefore, the two countries that are often talked about in relation to their role with Iran, in my view, are not involved in this matter.", Trump added.

Trump meanwhile, warned that if Russia or China were to take such a step, "it would be very bad for them" and "not in their interests".

Trump's remarks stand in contrast to Zelenskyy's allegations that Russia is helping Iran through satellite intelligence.

Moscow and Beijing have so far not issued an official response to the Ukrainian president's claims.

World.title: Russian strikes across Ukraine kill at least eight over last 24 hours
World.content:
Russian strikes across Ukraine have killed at least eight people and injured dozens more over the last 24 hours.

 

On Sunday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said one person was killed and nine were wounded in a drone attack on the northeastern city of Kharkiv.

"All the necessary emergency services have been deployed at the site," Zelenskyy said, adding that residential buildings had been hit.

In the Dnipropetrovsk region, two women aged 35 and 74 were killed after Russia struck three districts in the area with drones, artillery, and aerial bombs on Saturday, per local authorities.

One person died and 12 were hurt after further Russian strikes on Zaporizhzhia Oblast in southeastern Ukraine.

Ivan Fedorov, the head of the Zaporizhzhia Regional Military Administration, said on Sunday morning that Russian forces had launched 1,029 strikes on 50 settlements in the region over the last day.

On Sunday, Fedorov said there were reports of another fatality following a Russian attack.

Another two people were reportedly killed and 24 were injured in Kherson Oblast this weekend.

"Russian forces struck critical and social infrastructure, as well as residential areas in the region’s settlements; in particular, they damaged 18 high-rise blocks and 17 private houses," Oleksandr Prokudin, who heads the Kherson Regional Military Administration, wrote in a post on Telegram. "The occupiers also destroyed a church, a petrol station, shops, gas pipelines, a farm building, private garages and cars".

In Sumy Oblast in northern Ukraine, a 53-year-old man was killed and eight people were wounded following Russian attacks.

It comes as Ukrainian authorities reported a hit on a shopping centre in Kryvyi Rih on Sunday. A fire reportedly broke out at an Epitsentr DIY store following the strike.

Kazakh leader calls for end to war

Kazakhstan's President Qasym-Jomart Toqayev on Saturday reportedly told his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin that he should end his war in Ukraine.

"It is a shame, young people are dying... All this has to be stopped," Tokayev said, per AFP.

Responding to the news on social media, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha thanked Toqayev for his "realistic, timely, and wise message."

"Ukraine has proposed stopping the war along current frontlines and turning to diplomacy, but the Kremlin continues to reject this clear path to peace," Sybiha said in a statement posted to X.

Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov had already pushed back at Tokayev's comments, telling Interfax earlier on Saturday that it was "impossible" to "freeze" the war at the current time.

North Korea

Zelenskyy also warned in a video address on Saturday evening that Moscow was pushing for North Korea to send another 30,000 troops to support the Russian war effort in Ukraine.

Russian, left, and North Korea's servicemen attend the Victory Day military parade in Moscow, Saturday, May 9, 2026. AP photo

The Ukrainian leader said Russia has been making preparations to receive them in the Voronezh region since June and that Pyongyang was also looking to deliver additional launchers for ballistic missiles.

"This is a threat not only to Ukraine," Zelenskyy said. "Russia is helping North Korea learn how to wage war, improve its weapons, and gain real combat experience in using them. All of this is a threat to everyone in Asia who is within range of North Korean missiles".

North Korea has been providing troops to support Russia's full-scale invasion since the autumn of 2024, when they were first deployed in Russia's Kursk Oblast.

World.title: Israel's move to recognise Armenian genocide stalls under regional pressure
World.content:
The Israeli parliament's decision to postpone a vote on recognising the Armenian genocide by Ottoman Turkey is being seen as a triumph for regional diplomacy, as Azerbaijan in particular seeks to avert a further escalation in tensions between its close allies.

Advertising

The Israeli government gave no official reason for postponing the vote to formally recognise the Armenian genocide by Ottoman Turkey during World War I, which would have ratified a motion approved by the cabinet last month.

Ankara strongly denies the deaths of hundreds of thousands of Armenians constitute genocide.

While the motion's architect, Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar, called recognition a “moral duty”, critics say the move took aim at Turkey amidst rising tensions.

Based in Tbilisi, Israeli defence and security expert Eugene Kogan claims Israel badly miscalculated. “Foreign Minister Sa'ar could have waited and not just dropped a bomb that led to different repercussions coming from different sides,” he said.

Armenia, which is seeking to normalise ties with Turkey, reacted coolly, with Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan saying he saw no need to comment. Meanwhile, Israel’s close ally Azerbaijan reportedly lobbied Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to drop the motion.

“At the end of the day, it might be either dropped or dismissed, and it will not come again to the new parliament agenda,” predicted Kogan.

The Knesset dissolved on 17 July and won't reconvene until after elections scheduled for 27 October.

Israel's recognition of the Armenian genocide unsettles Turkey and Azerbaijan

Azerbaijan's influence

The Israeli newspaper Haaretz reported that pressure from Azerbaijan tipped the scales, though officials deny it.

Azerbaijan supplies nearly 40 percent of Israel’s oil and is a major customer for Israeli arms. The two countries’ partnership involves frequent Israeli ministerial visits and strong military cooperation, especially crucial for Israel given Azerbaijan’s border with Iran.

Baku also maintains a deep alliance with Ankara, summed up in the phrase “one nation, two states”. As Israeli-Turkish tensions flare over the Gaza conflict and Ankara’s support for Hamas, Azerbaijan is walking a diplomatic tightrope.

Zaur Gasimov, a Caucasus expert at Istanbul’s Turkish-German University, believes Baku viewed the Israeli genocide motion as a direct threat to its difficult balancing act.

“I can imagine that there were negotiations and talks on various levels between political elites of both countries,” he said. “For Israel, Azerbaijan is still of paramount importance. I would even say it's much more significant than it used to be with regard to the situation in and around Iran. So Baku was and is maybe the key intermediary between Israel and the Republic of Turkey.”

In what may be a calculated move to turn up the heat on Israel, Azerbaijan’s President Ilham Aliyev welcomed Palestinian Prime Minister Mohammad Mustafa this month. It was the first visit by a Palestinian leader since 2011.

“They [Israel] perceive it with a great sense of caution,” claimed analyst Kogan. “They don't know exactly what came out of this particular meeting between Aliyev and the Palestinian prime minister. And so there is a lot of guessing games right now taking place in both Tel Aviv and Jerusalem about the outcome.”

Such ambiguity over Baku’s intentions could strengthen its diplomatic hand, he suggested: “If Aliyev is involved in this Palestinian issue directly and no longer indirectly, it makes the situation very different for the Israelis.”

Turkey warns it could be Israel's 'next enemy' as tensions escalate

Syrian precedent

Baku is already leveraging its strong relationships with both Israel and Turkey to cool tempers.

“We have organised meetings between Turkey and Israel in Baku, specifically at the very beginning of the change of the Assad regime in Syria, where both parties had their own legitimate concerns,” said Hikmet Hajiyev, chief foreign policy adviser to the Azerbaijani president.

Syria is viewed as a potential flashpoint, with Israel and Turkey having a military presence. One tangible outcome of Azeri-brokered talks was the establishment last year of a military hotline in Syria, providing a rare glimmer of hope as tensions continue to mount.

“It's not unavoidable that Israel and Turkey will reach confrontation. I think we can stop this process,” argued Gallia Lindenstrauss, a specialist in Turkish foreign policy at Tel Aviv University's Institute for National Security Studies.

“They have a hotline between the Israeli Air Force and the Turkish Air Force, making sure that we will not have a collision in the skies of Syria, because we know both air forces are operating there. And the hotline has managed to keep the situation quiet. If I'm trying to find some anchor of reassurance that Turkish-Israeli relations can be controlled, it's Syria.”

As Israel approaches elections, a temporary lull in Turkish-Israeli tensions is anticipated. Still, since the main opposition shares the government’s concerns over Turkey, relations are set to remain fraught.

World.title: Wildfires spread in France and Spain forcing more to flee
World.content:
Spain's prime minister warned of "difficult hours ahead," as France's interior minister called the blaze near Bordeaux "unpredictable." Evacuations in both countries continued as high winds keep fires moving.

Massive wildfires in France and Spain continued to gather strength overnight with yet more evacuations for residents near France's western Bordeaux and Spain's capital Madrid.

A new fire outside the Spanish coastal town of Valencia claimed one life and forced residents to flee.

What is the latest on the French wildfires?

French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez on Sunday said that the blaze raging in the Gironde region near popular Bordeaux had become "extremely intense and unpredictable again" overnight.

Some 2,500 firefighters as well as 1,500 military personnel and 1,200 police have been deployed to the region.

New overnight evacuations brought the total number of displacements in France to over 220,000.

In Bordeaux, a convention center has been converted into a makeshift shelter for some of the hundreds of thousands of residents forced to flee raging wildfires Image: Margot Le Gonidec/ABACAPRESS/IMAGO

Fires near Bordeaux — a city of 268,000 residents — have also blocked roads, including a highway along the Atlantic coast, and halted train service near the major wine producing city.

In all, the fires have consumed some 42,000 hectares (103,000 acres) — an area four times the size of Paris, or seven times the size of Manhattan — laying waste to more land than at any time since 1949, when fires destroyed 50,000 hectares.

Separately, firefighters are battling an active fire in the southern Var region, where 3,000 people have been evacuated.

Fires west of Madrid also spread overnight, forcing the evacuation of eight municipalities Image: Cesar Manso/AFP

New Valencia fire in Spain killed one before being brought under control

In neighboring Spain, fires continued to consume areas west and north of the capital Madrid, where tens of thousands of people have been forced to flee their homes.

On Saturday, authorities ordered the evacuation of eight municipalities near Toledo.

A new fire raging outside the seaside town of Valencia killed one individual before firefighters could get it under control.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez on Sunday said, "difficult hours lie ahead" as he toured areas impacted by fire west of the capital, before adding "positive" developments had been seen in containing the fire overnight.

World.title: Germany classifies Berlin Pride ramming as 'terror attack'
World.content:
07/26/2026 July 26, 2026 Attack fuels security debate across German political spectrum

The attack on Berlin's Christopher Street Day (CSD) event has triggered strong reactions across Germany's political spectrum, with leaders condemning the violence while offering sharply different assessments of its causes and implications.

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier described the incident as an assault on the country's fundamental values.

"This act is an attack on our open society, on our way of life and on our ability to live together," he said.

Steinmeier added he was, "shaken and outraged."

How has the conservative CDU reacted?

The incident has also reignited debate over Germany's security policies and counterterrorism measures. Senior politicians from the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) called for tougher measures in response.

Günter Krings, the party's spokesperson on interior affairs, argued that harsher penalties should be introduced if investigators determine the attack was motivated by Islamist extremism. Speaking to the Rheinische Post he also suggested that citizenship rules could be tightened.

Fellow CDU lawmaker Alexander Throm urged lawmakers to move quickly on pending security legislation, which includes provisions for expanded digital investigative powers and retention of IP addresses for criminal investigations.

Reactions from center-left SPD, far-right AFD

Vice Chancellor Lars Klingbeil, co-leader of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), focused on defending the values represented by Pride events.

"Christopher Street Day stands for the right of every person to live freely," he said. "We will defend that."

Meanwhile, politicians from the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) used the incident to criticize the government's handling of security issues.

AfD lawmaker Martin Hess described it as "a complete failure of the government's security policies," arguing that authorities had failed to prevent violence despite extensive security preparations.

AfD lawmaker Thorsten Weiss claimed that Berlin faces a serious problem with “Islamist extremism” and called for an emergency committee meeting to investigate how a person he described as a known extremist was allegedly able to carry out the attack.

World.title: Can Pakistan-administered Kashmir elections calm tensions?
World.content:
Pakistan-administered Kashmir heads to the polls after weeks of deadly protests over seats reserved for displaced people from India-administered Kashmir. One local group has called for the elections to be boycotted.

The first phase of local elections in Pakistan-administered Kashmir is scheduled for Monday, July 27, amid calls for a boycott from the recently outlawed Jammu Kashmir Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), a grassroots alliance of civil society groups.

The JAAC has been demanding the abolition of 12 seats in the regional assembly reserved for people displaced from India-administered Kashmir and living in Pakistan. The group argues that only residents of Pakistan-administered Kashmir should be eligible to contest regional elections.

The dispute escalated after the Supreme Court of Pakistan-administered Kashmir ruled that the refugee seats are constitutionally protected and cannot be abolished without a constitutional amendment.

The regional government outlawed the JAAC in June under anti-terrorism laws, citing threats to public order, and detained dozens of its supporters.

The ban came amid rising tensions over the refugee seats and ahead of violent protests sparked by the group's campaign to scrap them.

The unrest has left around 30 people dead since June, according to local estimates cited by Reuters news agency.

India and Pakistan both claim Kashmir in its entirety, but each country only controls a section of the territory, making the Muslim-majority region a longstanding flash point between the nuclear-armed neighbors since their independence from Britain in 1947.

Protests cast shadow over vote

Since early June, Pakistan-administered Kashmir — known locally as Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) — has witnessed weeks of protests and sit-ins. While the dispute over the refugee seats has become a major issue, JAAC has also campaigned for broader economic and governance reforms.

Following the unrest, authorities split polling into three phases, with voting in Mirpur set for July 27 and elections in the protest-hit Poonch division postponed until August 10.

Voting in the regional capital, Muzaffarabad, has been delayed until August 2 over security concerns. The JAAC continues to stage a sit-in in Rawalakot, near the Line of Control with India.

Demand for fair representation

A major question is whether the elections can restore public confidence or merely offer a temporary pause in public anger.

"We are just asking for fair representation, which is our right," Ali Raza, a 22-year-old student protester in Rawalakot, told DW. "The local people who live here should have the right to choose their representatives, not the refugees who settled here from India."

"The election is a major opportunity for the people of AJK to choose their representatives," said Shazia Marri, the central information secretary of the Pakistan People's Party, which currently rules the region. "The people want their rights protected, their issues addressed and a government that delivers on its promises."

Unrest keeps flaring up in Pakistan-administered Kashmir To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

However, JAAC leaders argue that elections alone cannot resolve the issues that brought thousands of people onto the streets.

"Our movement is not replacing one government with another over time; we need our rights, but there are just political slogans in the campaigns," one JAAC official told DW under condition of anonymity.

Imran Khan, a geopolitical expert and former director of the US Institute of Peace Pakistan, expects the movement to continue post-elections.

"While elections in AJK are important on their own merit and for the continuity of the political process, they will not address the political grievances and demands of the people who are supporting JAAC," Khan, no relation to Pakistan's former prime minister, told DW. "The protest is outside the assembly. They no longer trust those institutions fully."

Has JAAC changed Kashmir's political landscape?

Analysts have said the JAAC protests marked a significant shift in Pakistan-administered Kashmir's politics by bringing together citizens across party lines around economic and governance issues rather than traditional political rivalries.

For Khan, JAAC is a dominant political force in quite significant parts of Pakistan-administered Kashmir.

"They have more street credibility than mainstream politicians and parties despite the allegations of foreign backing and funding. For now, they have disrupted the status quo politics in AJK," Khan said, noting that the Pakistani establishment has the means and methods to break up such political movements.

Experts caution that rebuilding trust will require more than campaign promises.

"[The] next government in AJK will be very weak, as it will be sandwiched between pressure from both the Pakistani establishment that controls AJK through administrative and security framework and the sentiment on the street, which is very pro JAAC," argued Khan. The next government would have "little credibility and limited room to govern unless it reaches an understanding with JAAC to ease political tensions."

But Marri of the Pakistan People's Party believes trust is rebuilt by listening to people's concerns, delivering practical solutions and empowering elected institutions.

Will protests return if reforms stall?

If key grievances remain unresolved, analysts warn that another wave of protests cannot be ruled out.

"It is too early to say that more waves of protests will be seen, but JAAC has the potential to become a lasting political force," said Khan, who suggested the group risks being weakened by internal divisions and pressure from the establishment.

"For now, both sides are treading carefully, with JAAC relying on mass support and the establishment avoiding a full crackdown while buying time," Khan added.

Kashmir tourism struggles post Pahalgam attack To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

While the vote will determine who governs Pakistan-administered Kashmir, it is unlikely to resolve the broader constitutional dispute over Kashmir or eliminate long-standing frustrations with the region's governance.

"Governments must listen to public concerns and address them through dialogue and effective governance. Stability comes from listening to people, respecting the law, and delivering results," Marri added.

For Raza, the Gen Z protester, "the world has changed, and we have seen governments toppling through student protests in the neighboring countries; we won't stop, and protests will continue until our rights have been given to us."

Edited by: Keith Walker

World.title: Sudan civil war: Civilians used as 'human shields'
World.content:
The situation in the besieged city of El Obeid in Sudan is worsening by the day, with rights organizations warning of mass atrocities. Children are traumatized and do not dare go to school.

Flattened houses and rubble where a school once stood: These are the scenes that have appeared in footage of the Sudanese city of El Obeid published by Ayin Network, a nonpartisan Sudanese media outlet. Drone attacks by the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have caused enormous damage to civilian infrastructure, including power grids, transformers, water treatment plants, schools, universities and hospitals in the capital of North Kordofan.

The local population is struggling to survive, according to Ahmed Awad, project manager for the UK children's rights organization Plan International, and a native of El Obeid. The city — whose population previously numbered half a million but has now become home to several hundred thousand internally displaced persons (IDP) — is under siege, he added.

There is a shortage of medical supplies as well as food and safe, clean water, and Awad said he saw long queues of IDPs at just one water pump: "Sometimes you can spend all day to get one liter of water for two or three days."

He added that a drone had hit a primary school and killed three children, which had caused trauma among other children, many of whom no longer dared go to school.

"One of the mothers said three of her children cannot sleep because always they are in fear of something happening again," he said, adding that Plan International tried "to provide psychosocial support" for people scared of drones that could hit a classroom at any time.

Sudan's civil war — the limits of humanitarian aid To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

El Obeid: trading hub in the desert

El Obeid is a strategically important location. The city is a trading hub in the middle of the desert on the only major route between Sudan's capital, Khartoum — which is controlled by the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) — and the western Darfur region, large parts of which are under the control of the RSF. Since the war began in 2023, the city has been captured by the RSF and recaptured by the army and allied militias many times.

El Obeid is currently controlled by the army, which has some 13,000 soldiers stationed there, and has been on the front line since fighting shifted from Darfur to Kordofan at the beginning of the year. The RSF has deployed troops to about 30 kilometers (18.6 miles) beyond the city limits, and has been using drones to bomb civilian infrastructure.

DW Documentary 'Sudan: A hospital in the shadow of war' To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

'Hallmarks of genocide'

Analysts, aid organizations and the United Nations have warned that the RSF could soon capture El Obeid. They fear a similar scenario to that which unfolded in the city of El Fasher in the neighboring state of North Darfur in October 2025, when the RSF began by bombing infrastructure before storming the city after an 18-month siege.

Earlier this year, a UN Fact-Finding Mission for the Sudan presented to the United Nations Human Rights Council in Geneva detailed atrocities in the capture of the El Fasher and identified "hallmarks of genocide."

A joint appeal issued by several human rights organizations warned that an escalation of the situation could lead to a repeat of atrocities and human rights violations, as documented in El Fasher. "We are alarmed by the ongoing hostilities around the city, including frequent drone strikes," said Pekka Haavisto, the UN secretary general's personal envoy for Sudan, in June: "These are already affecting the civilians and affecting humanitarian aid to the city. Any further escalation of the situation would place thousands of people at risk."

Who are Sudan's RSF? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Schools and hospitals turned into barracks

Adam Mousa Eshag, director of the Sudanese organization Darfur Victims Support Organization (DVS), is currently based in Kampala, the capital of Uganda. He is in constant contact with people in Sudan and El Obeid for his research, for which he also spoke to SAF soldiers. He explained that one reason the RSF was bombing schools is that SAF soldiers had turned classrooms into barracks.

He said that this was also the case in El Fasher, when the army "used schools and even hospitals as barracks." He said soldiers were repeating this scenario in El Obeid and that was "the problem," as when the RSF attacked, "civilians paid the price" because they were being used as "human shields."

Francesco Lanino, deputy country director of Save the Children in Sudan, said the drone strikes targeting schools and IDP camps were causing severe trauma. "We met several children who refused to talk," he said, reporting on a recent visit to the Tawila IDP camp near El Fasher. "It's hard for them to understand why all of this is happening."

This article was translated from German.

World.title: Middle East: No fresh US strikes on Iran for a second day
World.content:
Skip next section Yemen's Houthis say they downed Saudi reconnaissance drone

07/26/2026 July 26, 2026 Yemen's Houthis say they downed Saudi reconnaissance drone

Iran-backed Houthi rebels on Sunday said they had shot down Saudi Arabia's reconnaissance drone over the northwest of Yemen.

The Houthis "successfully shot down a Turkish-made... armed reconnaissance drone belonging to the Saudi enemy while it was carrying out hostile operations," the Yemeni group's military spokesman Yahya Saree said in a statement on X.

It comes a day after the Houthis claimed responsibility for attacks on oil facilities in Saudi Arabia.

The rising tension in the Red Sea has heightened concerns over further disruptions to global shipping.

The Houthis have said they would close the Bab el Mandeb strait, the southern gateway to the Red Sea, to Saudi-linked shipping, in retaliation for the Gulf kingdom's blockade on Yemen and a recent attack on the international airport in Sanaa, Yemen's rebel-held capital.

World.title: Vietnamese vessel sinks in South China Sea, 17 missing
World.content:
A Vietnamese-registered cargo ship carrying 62 crew members sank near Yongshu Reef in the South China Sea, one of the world's most important and contested maritime spaces.

Rescuers were searching on Sunday for 17 people missing after a Vietnamese ship sank in the South China Sea, China's ⁠state media reported.

Authorities in the Chinese island province of Hainan said the cargo vessel Khoi ​Nguyen 18 ran into trouble near Yongshu Reef, also known as Fiery Cross Reef, state broadcaster CCTV said.

The ship was carrying 62 crew members, and 45 people were rescued from the water.

Vietnamese authorities arrived at the scene immediately after the cargo ship "sank while operating in bad weather conditions in the East Sea," Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Pham Thu Hang said in a statement to AFP news agency.

What we know about the sinking incident

A Chinese rescue ship, the Nanhai Jiu 115, first spotted what was believed to be a distress flare from the vessel shortly before 6:30 pm on Saturday (1030 GMT).

The Khoi Nguyen 18 is a Vietnamese-registered ship measuring just under 70 meters (230 feet) in length, according to state news agency Xinhua.

It added that six Chinese vessels, a rescue helicopter and a Vietnamese vessel were involved in the search-and-rescue operations.

Hang said that authorities and fishing vessels were "actively searching for the remaining people."

How a small, disputed island wards off China's power claims To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Territorial disputes in South China Sea

Beijing claims sovereignty over almost the entire South China Sea, despite the 2016 international ruling, initiated by the Philippines against China, that its assertion has no legal basis.

One of the most highly contested areas is the ​Spratly Islands, which China calls the Nansha Islands, where China has built runways ⁠and militarized artificial islands.

But ​Beijing's sweeping claims to the busy waterway overlap with those of other countries, including Vietnam, the Philippines, Brunei, Malaysia and Taiwan.

World.title: Berlin CSD: Latest in string of deadly vehicle attacks
World.content:
The attack at a Berlin Pride event is only the most recent incident on a long list where vehicles were used as weapons. The US, Canada, and China also saw similar attacks in recent years.

Berlin, Germany, July 25, 2026

A Christopher Street Day event in the German capital, which attracts thousands of people every year, was attacked on Saturday night by a 21-year-old suspect who police said was associated with the "Islamist scene" in Berlin. One person was killed and another 16 people were injured, while the suspect, named as Abdul B., fled the scene.

Leipzig, Germany, May 4, 2026

Two people were killed and 20 more injured in early May when a car drove through a crowd in the eastern German city of Leipzig. The suspect in the case was described as a 33-year-old German national and local resident, who had been known to police, though not for relevant offenses.

Mannheim, Germany, March 3, 2025

At least two people were killed and several were injured in the southwestern German city of Mannheim in 2025 when a motorist intentionally drove his car into a crowd of people, according to police and public prosecutors. Authorities identified the suspect as a 40-year-old German man. Law enforcement ruled out a political motive at the time, though the man had paid a fine under Germany's hate crime laws for a comment he made on a social media platform in 2018.

Emergency services work at the scene after a car drove into a crowd in Munich in February 2025 Image: Michaela Stache/AFP

Munich, Germany, February 13, 2025

A 37-year-old woman and her two-year-old daughter were killed in Munich in February last year when a car was rammed into a demonstration organized by the trade union Verdi. A 25-year-old Afghan man subsequently went on trial for their murder, as well as the attempted murder of the dozens of other people injured in the attack.

New Orleans, United States, January 1, 2025

A vehicle plowed into a crowd of New Orleans revelers early on New Year's Day 2025, killing 14 people and injuring dozens of others. The driver of the vehicle and two police officers were killed in a firefight soon after the attack, which took place at about 3:15 in the morning local time. The FBI said it was investigating the incident as an act of terrorism.

Magdeburg, Germany, December 20, 2024

At least six people died and more than 300 were injured when a man slammed a rented BMW SUV into a Christmas market in eastern Germany. The suspect, who was arrested at the scene, was a 50-year-old doctor originally from Saudi Arabia who had expressed anti-Muslim views and support for the far-right AfD party. In June 2026, he was sentenced to life in prison, with the court noting the severity of his crime, which more or less rules out the possibility of an early release.

The suspect in the Magdeburg attack is alleged to have hired a BMW SUV to carry it out Image: Axel Schmidt/REUTERS

Zhuhai, China, November 11, 2024

A 62-year-old driver rammed a small SUV into people exercising at a sports complex in southern China on November 11, 2024, killing 38 people in the country's deadliest act of mass homicide in years. Another 48 were injured. Authorities said the perpetrator was upset about his divorce but offered few other details about his motive. The man was detained and sentenced to death, and executed in January 2025.

London, Canada, June 6, 2021

Four members of a Muslim family who were out for a walk were killed when an attacker hit them with a pickup truck in what then Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau called "a terrorist attack, motivated by hatred." The 23-year-old white nationalist attacker was sentenced to life in prison.

The London Ontario attacker killed four members of the same family and united the Muslim community in grief Image: Ian Willms/Getty Images

Toronto, Canada, April 23, 2018

A 25-year-old Canadian man drove a rented van into mostly female pedestrians on the main thoroughfare in Toronto, killing 10 people and injuring 16. He told police he belonged to the online "incel" community of sexually frustrated men. He was sentenced to life in prison with no possibility of parole for 25 years.

New York, United States, October 31, 2017

An Uzbek national killed eight people and seriously injured 12 others when he swerved a rented pickup truck on a bike path in New York City. Reportedly spurred on by a call to action by militant group "Islamic State," he was sentenced to eight consecutive life sentences plus an additional 260 years in prison.

Barcelona, Spain, August 17, 2017

A man driving a van plowed into people on the Spanish city's crowded Las Ramblas boulevard, killing 14 and injuring many more.

The "Islamic State" claimed responsibility, with members of the same cell carrying out a similar vehicle attack in the nearby resort town of Cambrils before being shot dead by police.

The perpetrator of the Ramblas attack was killed by police on August 21 after spending several days on the run.

Police in Spain embarked on a manhunt after the attack, with the suspect shot dead days later Image: Getty Images/C. Court

Charlottesville, United States, August 12, 2017

A white supremacist intentionally drove his car into a crowd of protesters who were opposing a "Unite the Right" rally, killing one woman and injuring dozens of people. He was sentenced to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole.

London, United Kingdom, March to June, 2017

The year 2017 saw a spate of vehicle attacks in the British capital starting on March 22, when a 52-year-old UK-born man rammed an SUV into people on Westminster Bridge, killing four before stabbing a policeman to death. The perpetrator — who was a convert to Islam — claimed to be waging jihad in revenge for Western military action in Muslim countries. He was shot dead.

On June 3, three Islamist attackers drove a van at pedestrians on London Bridge before stabbing people at the city's Borough Market. Eight people were killed and police killed the attackers.

The attackers on London Bridge went on to kill more people at the nearby Borough Market Image: Reuters/S. Wermuth

Later that month, on June 19, a 47-year-old man radicalized by far-right ideas drove a van at worshippers outside a mosque in London's Finsbury Park area, killing one man and injuring 15 people.

Melbourne, Australia, January 20, 2017

Six people were killed and more than 30 injured when a car hit lunchtime crowds at a pedestrian mall in Australia's second-largest city. The perpetrator was found to have been in a state of drug-induced psychosis.

Berlin, Germany, December 19, 2016

A rejected asylum-seeker from Tunisia drove a hijacked truck into a Christmas market in the German capital, killing 13 people and injuring dozens. The attacker was killed days later in a shootout in Italy. The attack was claimed by the "Islamic State" militant group.

Nice, France, July 14, 2016

A Tunisian-born French resident drove a rental truck for nearly 2 kilometers along a seaside promenade crowded with tourists. The attack on the French Riviera resort, which took place on France's Bastille Day holiday, killed 86 people — the deadliest of its kind.

(AFP, AP, dpa, Reuters)

This article was first published on April 8, 2025, and updated on July 26, 2026.

World.title: India news: Modi announces task force to reform exams
World.content:
07/26/2026 July 26, 2026 Modi announces exam reform task force after protests

Prime Minister Narendra Modi has announced a special task force to overhaul the country's examination system after days of student-led protests over alleged exam paper leaks.

"Our examination system should be trustworthy, should be transparent and the system should make maximum use of technology," Modi said on Instagram, adding that new legislation to deal with paper leaks would be introduced in Parliament on Monday.

Modi added the government would set up a "high-powered task force" focused on examination reform.

The panel will be led by Infosys co-founder Nandan Nilekani.

The demonstrations drew thousands to New Delhi's Jantar Mantar site and became one of the largest anti-government protests in India in recent years.

The movement, organized by the social media-driven Cockroach Janta Party, led to the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.

Protest organizers called off the demonstrations on Saturday following his departure.

World.title: Los incendios de Madrid, Ávila y Toledo obligan a evacuar o confinar a 90.000 personas
World.content:
El incendio de Ávila es ya el mayor de la historia de España con 50.000 hectáreas afectadas. El Gobierno declarará este martes las zonas afectadas como gravemente dañadas por la emergencia

Los grandes incendios forestales que arrasan la provincia de Ávila y la Comunidad de Madrid siguen activos y fuera de capacidad de extinción. Sí se han logrado contener muchos de los frentes, aunque se mantienen activas “varias cabezas” y no pueden darse por perimetrados. Desde hace cuatro días, las fuertes rachas de viento dificultan la extinción y los bomberos encadenan jornadas de trabajo extenuantes. Los esfuerzos del operativo están este domingo centrados de nuevo en proteger poblaciones, evacuar de forma preventiva y evitar que las llamas de ambos se fusionen. Aun así, la Unidad Militar de Emergencias (UME) los trata y coordina como un único fuego, y el Gobierno ha ampliado la emergencia nacional a Toledo. Entre las tres regiones, hay afectadas ya 77.000 hectáreas y alrededor de 90.000 evacuados o confinados, según los últimos datos de Interior, que rebajan ligeramente la cifra estimada el sábado por la noche por las autoridades madrileñas. Solo en Ávila, son 50.000 hectáreas, lo que lo convierte en el mayor incendio de la historia de España.

La clave durante el día está siendo, otra vez, el viento, y las previsiones son más favorables. El optimismo, aunque mayor, es todavía contenido. “Quedan horas complejas, pero la noche ha sido muy positiva” en la “lucha” contra el incendio, ha resumido el presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez, desde el puesto de mando de Castilla y León, ubicado en Navaluenga, donde también ha anunciado que el Gobierno declarará este martes como gravemente dañadas por la emergencia las zonas afectadas por los incendios.

Desde el municipio madrileño de Villamanta, los Reyes han destacado la “coordinación ejemplar” de autoridades y ciudadanos: “Unidos se puede afrontar cualquier riesgo”. En esa localidad siguen realojados decenas de vecinos evacuados de varias zonas del suroeste de la región. “Lo han pasado muy mal. Algunos llevan cuatro días fuera de sus casas, han perdido muchos bienes y hemos perdido un patrimonio natural incalculable”, ha lamentado el rey Felipe VI, acompañado de la ministra para la Transición Ecológica y el Reto Demográfico, Sara Aagesen, y la presidenta de la Comunidad de Madrid, Isabel Díaz Ayuso. Sobre el futuro, “ya habrá tiempo para reflexionar sobre qué se puede hacer mejor”, ha apuntado.

02:20 La UME y los bomberos luchan contra los incendios durante la noche

La situación en el terreno la explicaba así el jefe del Primer Batallón de Intervención de la UME, el teniente coronel Alfonso Arribas: “Se ha avanzado bastante en los trabajos realizados en todo el perímetro, ya que la tarde fue bastante inestable, pero siempre adelantándonos a la situación. Ahora podríamos decir que todos los frentes están contenidos. Hay solo unas cabezas activas en las que se está trabajando y hoy esperamos que las condiciones nos permitan trabajar en todas esas zonas que están fuera de control, pero no es en todo el perímetro”, ha detallado en una entrevista en RTVE.

Hay cabida, por tanto, para cierto optimismo tras un sábado realmente complicado. “No ha sido un día positivo, no lo ha sido porque las condiciones meteorológicas han sido absolutamente difíciles, y si no ha ido a más, ha sido gracias al trabajo de todos los servidores [públicos]”, valoraba por la noche el ministro del Interior, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, tras la última reunión del Cecop.

Las labores de extinción continúan sin descanso con un objetivo claro: que las llamas del sur procedentes del incendio de Burgohondo, en Ávila, no confluyan con las que avanzaban desde Madrid. El jefe de la UME, el teniente general Francisco Javier Marcos Izquierdo, apuntó que solo se han juntado en un “frente discontinuo muy pequeño” en la localidad de San Martín de Valdeiglesias, que se encuentra entre los dos frentes. A pesar de ello, no se puede considerar todavía que se hayan convertido de facto en un solo megaincendio. La zona de separación entre las dos lenguas es de unos 15 kilómetros, según Marcos: “Creemos que hemos detenido el avance de las llamas en el interior de esos dos incendios, así como en el flanco este que podía rolar hacia Madrid. El perímetro está definido, pero no está consolidado”.

Todo dependerá, de nuevo, del viento. Las condiciones meteorológicas serán este domingo algo mejores que en los días previos y se esperan rachas menos fuertes. El sábado, en Ávila se registraron rachas por encima de los 50 kilómetros por hora y en Madrid superaron los 40, detalla Javier Armenteros, delegado de Agencia Estatal de Meteorología (Aemet) en la Comunidad de Madrid. “Hoy va a ser mucho más favorable en la meteorología: el viento ya no será fuerte”, pronostica. Aunque durante la noche sí se dieron rachas fuertes en las cumbres de las montañas de Ávila. El resto del día se espera que sean más débiles, y, aunque en general será de componente norte, “puede haber momentos en los que cambie de dirección”. El problema a la hora de hacer una previsión precisa es que “la magnitud del incendio perturba todo el entorno y crea sus propias condiciones meteorológicas”.

El presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez, este domingo en el puesto de mando avanzado en Navaluenga (Ávila). ÓSCAR CORRAL (EL PAÍS)

“Los bomberos han tenido incidencias, pero han podido trabajar”

El fuego que calcina hectárea tras hectárea de la Sierra Oeste de Madrid sigue sin estabilizarse ni perimetrarse, pese a que ha frenado su avance durante la noche. La madrugada ha permitido a los bomberos actuar en distintos frentes. “Los efectivos han tenido algunas incidencias con el viento porque ha soplado con rachas durante la noche en algún momento, pero han logrado trabajar”, detalla un portavoz de 112 Comunidad de Madrid a este periódico.

El delegado del Gobierno, Francisco Martín, ha explicado que, por el momento, el flanco oeste ha logrado contenerse y no avanza, y los trabajos se centran en enfriar progresivamente toda la zona quemada y en evitar reactivaciones. Los esfuerzos se concentran sobre todo en impedir que se reactiven los focos en el embalse de San Juan. En la región hay ya 12 municipios evacuados y cuatro confinados: en total son 29.609 las personas que duermen fuera de sus casas y 21.132 los aislados en sus pueblos.

El de Burgohondo (1.269 habitantes), en Ávila, también ha seguido comiendo terreno. Se mueve hacia el sur de la provincia y preocupa su avance en el Valle del Tiétar, que tuvo que ser desalojado. Allí se intensifican los trabajos de extinción desde el sábado y las labores de los bomberos desplazados se centran en proteger localidades. El presidente de la Junta de Castilla y León, Alfonso Fernández Mañueco, ha recordado que “este incendio se ha producido por una imprudencia”, y ha anunciado que la comunidad va a personarse como acusación contra quien haya iniciado el incendio. La Guardia Civil detuvo el viernes a una persona e investiga a otra por utilizar maquinaria pesada en una zona donde estaba prohibido su uso, lo que provocó una chispa que originó las llamas.

El incendio ha obligado a desalojar a 25.087 personas de 16 municipios y confinar a 8.735 de tres. Se prevé que los vecinos de más localidades reciban durante el día las alertas en sus teléfonos móviles para que abandonen sus pueblos y se dirijan a las zonas preparadas para acogerlos. A esto se suman los habitantes afectados en Toledo, también en emergencia nacional y hacia donde se dirige el fuego de Madrid: ya son 5.200 los desalojados en 11 localidades. Para muchos, esta noche ya ha sido la tercera fuera de casa y van camino de la cuarta.

World.title: La España rica de las urbanizaciones bosque siente cerca el peligro del fuego: “En algún momento nos puede pasar”
World.content:
Un motorista pasa este sábado al mediodía por delante de una rotonda donde se lee Boadilla del Monte, siempre verde.

Los municipios acomodados del oeste de Madrid han esquivado el avance del gran incendio en la región, pero temen que la amenaza vuelva en otro momento

El cielo de Boadilla del Monte se había despejado de ceniza este sábado por la mañana, casi nadie llevaba mascarilla y la gente había vuelto a las terrazas. Nada que ver con el día anterior, cuando el alcalde, Javier Úbeda, reconoce que pasaron un mal rato hasta que el viento cambió de dirección. El fuego del gran incendio que arrasa el suroeste de la Comunidad de Madrid ha afectado a pequeños pueblos de la zona rural, la más periférica de la región. De haber penetrado hacia la capital, las llamas hubieran afectado a los municipios acomodados y mucho más poblados como Villanueva de la Cañada, Villaviciosa de Odón o Boadilla, donde se asientan lo que algunos llaman urbanizaciones bosque, entornos privilegiados pero expuestos al peligro de los incendios.

“Hemos pasado momentos bastante tensos porque piensas que en algún momento nos puede pasar”, decía este sábado Melina Da Lolio, una vecina de la Urbanización El Bosque, de Villaviciosa de Odón, que daba un paseo en familia por Boadilla. “Ayer (por el viernes) tuvimos la televisión encendida todo el rato porque tenemos amigos afectados”.

Tan solo a 30 kilómetros de Boadilla se han producido evacuaciones, en municipios como Navalagamella. Aquí no se ha desatado el pánico, pero el episodio ha dejado mal cuerpo a algunos. “Noto hoy a la gente de Boadilla menos bien”, decía María Antonia Colado, de 76 años. “Es que estamos haciendo frontera”.

Varios comensales sentados este sábado a primera hora de la tarde en la terraza de Le Port, un restaurante con vistas al monte de Boadilla. FERNANDO PEINADO

Boadilla del Monte es el segundo municipio más rico de España y lleva décadas recibiendo a madrileños que buscan vivir cerca del entorno natural. El municipio dispone de casi 1.000 hectáreas de monte público y otras 1.000 de monte privado. Un eslogan del Ayuntamiento es “siempre verde”.

Todos los veranos esta ciudad de 66.349 habitantes se pone en alerta. La peor pesadilla es un incendio en el Monte de Boadilla, el orgullo de los vecinos. Por fortuna no ha habido grandes incendios en la localidad recientemente, aunque sí se recuerdan varios sustos. A principios de junio ardió un chalé por un incendio que comenzó en las plantas arizónicas que bordeaban la vivienda. La rápida intervención de los bomberos de la Comunidad impidió la propagación a otras parcelas.

Los incendios forestales que afectan a núcleos urbanos son una tragedia recurrente. El verano pasado murió una persona y salieron ardiendo varios chalés en otro municipio madrileño, Tres Cantos, cuando se desató un incendio que se propagó a velocidad de vértigo por el monte bajo. Y este verano la virulencia de varios incendios en España ha obligado a desalojar decenas de localidades.

El alcalde Úbeda, del Partido Popular, estaba reunido este sábado por la mañana en su despacho con varios mandos de policía y protección civil analizando la evolución de la catástrofe por si el Centro de Mando les pidiera ayuda para acoger a evacuados en un polideportivo climatizado.

El alcalde de Boadilla del Monte, Javier Úbeda, reunido este sábado por la mañana con varios responsables de seguridad del municipio. FERNANDO PEINADO

Para prevenir incendios, Boadilla recurre a ovejas bombero, que pastan entre diciembre y junio en el monte para que se coman la hierba seca que sirve de combustible al fuego. En verano, se activa un retén de los bomberos forestales en una finca del municipio, y desde hace unos días cuentan con un dron de vigilancia cuyas tareas van desde la prevención de incendio a la detección de personas perdidas.

Desde la oposición, el PSOE de Boadilla reconoce que el cuidado del monte es bueno, pero cree que podría ser mejor si el alcalde apoyara una larga reivindicación de los socialistas que consiste en la declaración de utilidad pública de todo ese espacio verde, la máxima protección posible. Ese catalogación, dicen, entregaría la responsabilidad a la Comunidad de Madrid, con más recursos, y además blindaría ese terreno frente a los “especuladores urbanísticos”.

El secretario de Medio Ambiente de los socialistas locales, Paco Fernández Castán, dice que debe haber mucha vigilancia porque el monte de Boadilla es una “joya”. “¿Qué otro municipio tiene un espacio forestal como el que tiene Boadilla a 14 kilómetros de la Puerta del Sol?“, se pregunta.

La respuesta rápida es clave. Por eso, algunas de estas urbanizaciones tienen la suerte de contar cerca con un parque de bomberos, como es el caso de La Finca de Pozuelo de Alarcón, el exclusivo complejo donde vive parte de la élite y celebridades de España. Cada cierto tiempo salta la noticia de que uno de estos chalés ha ardido.

La lucha contra el fuego también es responsabilidad de los vecinos de estas urbanizaciones. En los grupos de WhatsApp de La Cabaña, que pertenece a Pozuelo de Alarcón, los vecinos recuerdan la necesidad de cortar y regar las arizónicas, esos setos que protegen la intimidad y que son tan peligrosos porque se queman rápido cuando están secos. Precisamente por el riesgo de incendio, los ayuntamientos multan a los vecinos que descuidan sus jardines, un problema común cuando estos chalés no son habitados continuamente.

Con todo, el verdadero temor de los vecinos de La Cabaña son los pirómanos, dice una residente, Ana Castro. Han denunciado ya varios conatos de incendio provocados en el monte con el que conviven, Montegancedo, uno de los últimos pulmones verdes que le quedan a Pozuelo. Varios promotores inmobiliarios tienen una batalla legal contra los ecologistas, que han paralizado judicialmente sus planes. “Los vecinos organizamos rondas de vigilancia porque no nos fiamos”, dice Castro.
